ad: CASE OF GÖKÇE AND OTHERS v. TÜRKİYE
sonuc: Remainder inadmissible (Art. 35) Admissibility criteria;(Art. 35-1) Exhaustion of domestic remedies;Violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
paragraflar: CASE OF GÖKÇE AND OTHERS v. TÜRKİYE
(Applications nos. 51110/19 and 3 others –

Art 3 (substantive) • Degrading treatment • Placement of prisoners, detained on terrorism-related charges, in single cells, based on decisions of the prison administrations, and restrictions imposed on their contact with other prisoners • Given the cumulative effect of the conditions of detention, the third and fourth applicants were subjected to suffering exceeding the unavoidable level inherent in detention • Minimum level of severity not attained in relation to the first and second applicants
Prepared by the Registry. Does not bind the Court.
This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.
In the case of Gökçe and Others v. Türkiye,
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:
Arnfinn Bårdsen, President, Saadet Yüksel, Jovan Ilievski, Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir, Gediminas Sagatys, Juha Lavapuro, Hugh Mercer, judges, and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

the applications (nos. 51110/19, 34526/20, 48100/20, and 34616/21) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Turkish nationals (“the applicants”) on the various dates indicated in the appended table;
the decision to give notice to the Turkish Government (“the Government”) of the complaints concerning Article 3 of the Convention and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the applications;
the parties’ observations;
Having deliberated in private on 22 September 2026,
Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

1. The applications concern the applicants’ placement in single cells in prison and the restrictions imposed on their contact with other prisoners. The applicants complain of a violation of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the conditions and duration of the regime imposed on them.
2. A list of the applicants, indicating their years of birth, their places of residence and their representatives, is set out in the Appendix.
3. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye.
4. The facts of the cases, as submitted by the parties may be summarised as follows.

5. At the time of the events giving rise to the present applications, the applicants were detained in closed penal institutions, either awaiting trial or pending appeal proceedings. All applicants held public office at the time of their arrest and pre-trial detention on charges of membership of an armed terrorist organisation described by the Turkish authorities as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (Fetullahçı Terör Örgütü/Paralel Devlet Yapılanması – hereinafter referred to as “FETÖ/PDY”).

6. After they were placed in pre-trial detention, the applicants were initially held in multiple-occupancy cells in different prisons. On various dates during their pre-trial detention, the relevant prison administrations decided to transfer them from those multiple-occupancy cells and to place them in single cells.
THE APPLICANTS’ CONDITIONS OF DETENTION

7. The applicants were detained in different prisons and accommodated in single cells for varying periods of time, and their contact with other prisoners was restricted to varying degrees. The detailed circumstances of each applicant’s detention (including the dates, the prisons concerned, the size and material conditions of the cells in which they were held, their contact with the outside world, the restrictions imposed on their contact with other prisoners and on their access to the outdoor exercise yard, and the procedural steps taken in respect of their placement) are set out in paragraphs 10‑44 below.

8. The Government provided general information concerning the single cells in which the applicants had been held – including the dimensions of those cells. They submitted that the applicants’ cells had been equipped with a separate sanitary partition (containing a washbasin, toilet and shower), and that they had had access to cold and hot water on a daily basis. The cells had had a bed, mattress, wardrobe, table and chair. The applicants had been able to buy a television and a radio from the prison shop. They had had access to periodical and non-periodical publications. Their access to medical care had not been restricted, and they had had access to the prison doctor and had been transferred to State hospitals for treatment, if necessary.

9. Some applicants contested the information submitted by the Government, such as the material conditions and dimensions of the cells in which they had been held, the scope of the restrictions on their access to the outdoor yard, or their ability to maintain contact with other prisoners. In the description of the facts concerning each applicant below, the Court has taken note of the parties’ submissions and has indicated, where relevant, such disagreements.
Application no. 51110/19 (Musa Gökçe v. Türkiye)

10. The applicant in application no. 51110/19 (hereinafter referred to as “the first applicant”) was a public servant working at the Banking Regulation and Supervision Agency. On 30 September 2016 he was placed in pre-trial detention on charges of membership of FETÖ/PDY. From 30 September 2016 until his release on 14 July 2020, he was detained in Marmara no. 5 L-Type Prison.

11. On 17 April 2018 the prison’s internal administration and observation board decided to place the first applicant in a single cell. Referring to sections 9(2)(d-e), 24(1)(d), 113 and 116(1) of Law no. 5275 and Articles 69(1)(c-d) and 180(2) of the regulation on the management of prisons and the execution of sentences and preventive measures (see paragraphs 45 and 47-49 below), the board stated in its decision that, for administrative reasons and in view of the nature of the offence for which he had been detained, it was appropriate for the first applicant to be placed in one of the single or three-person cells. It further stated that his placement in a single cell aimed at ensuring both safety and order within the prison facility and the safety of the detainee himself, in the light of his former profession. It was noted that the first applicant’s right to visitation and to make telephone calls were not affected by this decision. The first applicant was then placed in a single cell and remained there until his release on 14 July 2020.

12. On 20 June 2018 the enforcement judge dismissed an objection lodged by the first applicant against the decision of the prison administration and observation board, finding that the prison administration had discretion regarding the placement of detainees and that the impugned measure was in accordance with the law. On 11 July 2018 the Silivri Assize Court dismissed an appeal by the first applicant against that decision. The first applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, alleging a violation of the prohibition of ill-treatment on account of his isolation in a single cell. On 26 November 2019 the Constitutional Court declared the first applicant’s individual application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, with reference to a previous decision that it had delivered in the case of Raşit Konya (see paragraphs 51-54 below).

13. According to the information provided by the parties, the first applicant was held alone in a single cell measuring 12 square metres (sq. m.). Following his placement there, he was confined for 21 hours a day, having access to the outdoor area for the remaining time. As to the amount of time spent outdoors the parties’ accounts broadly coincide: the Government submitted that the first applicant had had access to the outdoor area for three hours a day in the company of three other inmates, while the first applicant submitted that he had been taken out twice a day for one-and-a-half-hour periods in the company of two other prisoners. The parties disagreed, however, as to the conditions and character of the cell. The Government submitted that it had been adequately furnished, whereas the first applicant submitted that the cell had been of the same type as those used for detainees serving aggravated life sentences (ağırlaştırılmış müebbet hapis cezası) or undergoing disciplinary solitary confinement. According to the first applicant, the cell had been covered with drawings and graffiti left by previous inmates, and the bathroom and toilet had been located within a single space. The bathroom had had no ventilation, giving rise to serious odour, mould and damp, the sink had lacked a proper drainage system and had leaked, and the wardrobe had been broken and mouldy. The cell had had no cooling system and had been very hot during the summers. The first applicant added that his requests for those conditions to be improved had yielded no result, that the outdoor area to which he had been taken had been dirty, and that he had been able to access the grass football pitch for only one hour per week following the end of the state of emergency in July 2018. He had been checked by prison officers during the night and searched when going out to the yard. He contrasted this regime with that of his previous multi-occupancy cell, where there had been an exercise area that he had been free to enter and leave at will between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m.

14. Between 17 April 2018 and 14 July 2020, the first applicant was visited by his relatives and lawyers on 44 different days (with several relatives sometimes attending on the same day), and he had had telephone calls with his wife on 88 occasions. He was given 124 books during his detention, sat the national examination for admission to higher education in 2019 and was enrolled in a university programme that year.

15. During his imprisonment the first applicant consulted a general practitioner on 11 occasions and was transferred to State hospitals for further examination by neurology, cardiology, physiotherapy, ophthalmology and general surgery specialists on a further 11 occasions. These consultations covered the assessment and analysis of a herniated disc on the applicant’s back and the prescription of related medication. He underwent two assessments of his mental well-being during the admission procedure, which was conducted by specialists from the prison’s psycho-social support service. He received individual counselling from the prison’s psychologist on four occasions and he consulted a psychiatrist at a State hospital on two further occasions. The first applicant submitted that during his stay in the single cell, his pre-existing lumbar disc herniation had significantly deteriorated and he had developed severe psychological distress, manifesting in symptoms of clinical depression.
Application no. 34526/20 (Eşref Köse v. Türkiye)

16. At the time of his arrest, the applicant in application no. 34526/20 (hereinafter referred to as “the second applicant”) worked as a public prosecutor in Samsun. On 21 July 2016 he was arrested on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY. On the same day he was placed in pre-trial detention in Samsun E-Type Prison. On 15 November 2016 he was transferred to Bolu F-Type High-Security Prison and remained there until his transfer to an open prison on 13 October 2021.

17. On 19 September 2016, when he was still in Samsun E-Type Prison, he was placed in a single cell, pursuant to a decision taken by the prison administration. An objection lodged by the second applicant to that decision was rejected by the enforcement judge, who found it to be in accordance with the law. On 17 October 2016 the Samsun Assize Court rejected an objection lodged by the second applicant against the enforcement judge’s decision. The second applicant did not lodge an individual application with the Constitutional Court following that decision.

18. On 15 November 2016 the second applicant was transferred to Bolu F-Type High-Security Prison, where he was placed in a three-person cell with two other prisoners. On 18 November 2017 he was placed in a single cell by a decision of the prison administration, on the basis of a letter from the General Directorate to that effect and pursuant to sections 111(2), 113(1), 115(e) and 116 of Law no. 5275 (see paragraph 45 below). The decision stated that the second applicant was being held in pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of a terrorist organisation and that he was being placed in a single cell on security and administrative grounds. The second applicant lodged an objection against that decision with the Bolu enforcement judge.

19. On 14 March 2018 the enforcement judge dismissed the second applicant’s objection. In his decision, the enforcement judge reasoned that, pursuant to the Court’s decision in Bora v. Türkiye ((dec.), no. 30647/17, 28 November 2017), the second applicant’s accommodation in a single cell did not in itself attain the minimum level of severity required to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention. The judge noted that the second applicant was held in the same type of prison and under the same conditions as the applicant in Bora (cited above), that he was not subjected to the restrictions applicable to disciplinary solitary confinement, and that he continued to receive family visits and to have telephone calls with his relatives, and that he maintained access to radio, television and publications. The judge considered the measure to be proportionate and necessary in view of the offence imputed to the second applicant, the uncertainty as to his position within the FETÖ/PDY organisation’s hierarchy, the risk that accommodation with his co‑accused might lead to the commission of an offence, and the need to maintain the security of the institution. Reiterating the Court’s case-law to the effect that prohibiting contact with other detainees for reasons of security, discipline or protection does not in itself amount to inhuman treatment, he concluded that the impugned decision had been lawful.

20. On 6 June 2018 the Bolu Assize Court dismissed an objection lodged by the second applicant against the enforcement judge’s decision. The Assize Court firstly held that the legal provisions concerning the management of prisons allowed the second applicant to be accommodated in a high-security prison. Secondly, it noted that in the Bolu F-Type Prison, there were 103 three‑person cells and 61 single cells. Whether a prisoner accommodated in a high-security prison should be placed in a single or three-person cell was a matter concerning the organisation and order within that prison and constituted a decision ultimately falling to the discretion of the prison administration.

21. On 4 September 2018 the second applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, complaining that his placement in single cells in Samsun and Bolu prisons had violated the prohibition on ill-treatment. On 2 April 2020 the Constitutional Court declared the second applicant’s individual application inadmissible, stating that his complaints concerning the alleged violation of his fundamental rights and freedoms were manifestly ill-founded, and that the complaints also did not fulfil the other admissibility criteria foreseen in Law no. 6216 on the establishment and rules of procedure of the Constitutional Court. The court referred in this connection to its previous decisions in Raşit Konya and Timur Demir (see paragraphs 51‑56 below).

22. At Samsun Prison, from 19 September until 15 November 2016, the second applicant was held in a single cell measuring 15 sq. m. At Bolu Prison, from 18 November 2017 until his transfer to a multiple-occupancy cell on 8 October 2020, he was held in three successive single cells: the first two (in which he was held between 18 November 2017 and 1 November 2019) were designed to accommodate three persons and measured 50 sq. m., while the second (in which he was held from 1 November 2019) measured 11.4 sq. m. As regards the lighting of the cells in Bolu Prison, the second applicant submitted that the lights had been switched on and off during the night disturbing his sleep, while the Government submitted that a prison guard had been constantly present in the corridor and that a lighting button was placed there for the purpose of ensuring prisoners’ safety.

23. As regards outdoor exercise, after 26 October 2016 the second applicant was taken to the outdoor yard at Samsun for at least one hour a day in the company of two other prisoners. At Bolu Prison he was taken to the outdoor yard for one and a half hours a day in the company of another prisoner.

24. As regards contact with others, the second applicant submitted that during the first 39 days of his detention at Samsun he had not been allowed to communicate with anyone. The Government submitted that, between 19 September and 15 November 2016, the second applicant had been visited by his relatives and lawyers on five different days, with several relatives sometimes attending on the same day, and that he had had telephone calls with his wife. The parties broadly agreed that the second applicant had begun to take part in activities around May or June 2018. The second applicant submitted that he had been prohibited from engaging in any educational, rehabilitative or cultural activity until June 2018. The Government submitted that, from May 2018 onwards, he had participated at regular intervals – on 28 occasions in 2018, 56 occasions in 2019 and 10 occasions in 2020 – in social, sporting and conversational activities (participation in conversation groups and sporting activities on the grass pitch, the open pitch, the closed sports pitch and table tennis sessions) and that, after 7 June 2018, he had also taken part in psycho‑social and cultural activities – including meetings with a preacher (vaiz). The parties’ accounts also broadly corresponded as regards subsequently imposed restrictions: the second applicant submitted that he had been completely isolated from any contact with others between 8 September and 27 November 2018, while the Government submitted that the prison administration had restricted his participation in activities with other prisoners in September 2018, that that restriction had been set aside by the Bolu Assize Court on 16 November 2018, and that he had thereafter continued to take part in activities with other prisoners.

25. During his detention in single cells at Bolu Prison, between 18 November 2017 and 8 October 2020, the second applicant was visited by his relatives and lawyers on 115 different days, with several relatives sometimes attending on the same day, and he had telephone calls with his relatives on 128 occasions.

26. Following his transfer to Bolu Prison (see paragraph 16 above) the second applicant was diagnosed with anxiety and depression and received medication. He was examined and treated at the offices of the prison’s primary-healthcare physician and dentist on 40 occasions, consulted the prison psychologist and was transferred to a State hospital for consultation with a psychiatrist. The second applicant submitted that, as a result of the conditions of his detention, he had received psychological treatment and taken medication for a long period and had developed severe psychological problems.
Application no. 48100/20 (Süleyman Kul v. Türkiye)

27. At the time of his arrest, the applicant in application no. 48100/20 (hereinafter referred to as “the third applicant”) worked as a judge at the Court of Cassation. On 20 July 2016 he was arrested on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY. On the same day he was placed in pre-trial detention in Sincan T-Type Prison. On 8 October 2016 he was transferred to Marmara no. 4 L‑Type Prison where he was held until his release on 7 June 2023. According to the third applicant, he was placed in a single cell on the same day of his transfer. The Government submitted that the third applicant was placed in a single cell on 10 October 2016, without providing information about where he had been accommodated between 8 and 10 October 2016.

28. By a decision of 10 October 2016, Marmara Prison’s administration and observation board decided to place the third applicant in a single cell. Referring to sections 9(2)(d-e), 24(1)(d), 113 and 116(1) of Law no. 5275 and sections 69(1)(c-d) and 180(2) of the regulation on the management of prisons and the execution of sentences and preventive measures (see paragraphs 45 and 47-49 below), the board stated that, in view of the nature of the offence for which the third applicant had been detained, it was appropriate to place him in one of the single or three-person cells. His placement in such a cell was aimed at ensuring safety and order within the prison facility and the safety of the detainee himself, in the light of his former profession.

29. On 1 November 2016 the enforcement judge dismissed an objection lodged by the third applicant against the prison administration and observation board’s decision. The enforcement judge reasoned that by virtue of section 116 of Law no. 5275 (which referred back to section 9 of the same Law – see paragraph 45 below), statutory provisions concerning convicted prisoners and their placement in high-security prisons could also be applied to persons held in pre-trial detention, in so far as they were compatible with the status of pre-trial detention. The judge concluded that, in the light of those provisions, the prison administration was authorised to accommodate the third applicant in single or three-person cells within the high-security section of the prison. On 24 November 2016 the Silivri Assize Court rejected an objection by the third applicant against that decision. On 6 April 2020 the Constitutional Court declared the third applicant’s individual application – in which he had complained of a violation of the prohibition of ill-treatment on account of his isolation – inadmissible as being manifestly ill-founded, with reference to its Raşit Konya decision (see paragraphs 51-54 below).

30. The third applicant was held on his own in a single cell until his release on probation on 7 June 2023 (see paragraph 27 above) – a period of about six years and eight months. The parties disagreed as to the size and character of the cell: the Government submitted that it had measured 12.45 sq. m., whereas the third applicant submitted that it had measured 8 sq. m., had been originally designed for short-term disciplinary punishment, had had no kitchen, and had been of the type used for disciplinary punishment or for the accommodation of prisoners serving aggravated life imprisonment. The third applicant added that the cell had been cold during the winter.

31. The parties broadly agreed in respect of the third applicant’s outdoor exercise: both stated that, from October 2016 until 9 May 2018, he had had access to the outdoor area for one hour a day on his own, and that from that date onwards he had had access for two hours a day, in the company of two other prisoners. The third applicant submitted that from 2019 onwards he had been allowed to use the football pitch for 45 minutes each week. As regards lighting at night, the third applicant submitted that a spotlight directed into his cell from across the corridor had kept it permanently illuminated and that prison officers had carried out hourly checks during the night by opening the corridor door and switching on the lights – all of which had disrupted his sleep. The Government did not address those points.

32. Between 10 October 2016 and 7 June 2023 the third applicant was visited by his relatives and lawyers on 342 different days, with several relatives sometimes attending on the same day. He had telephone calls with relatives on 377 occasions. He borrowed 69 books during his detention, participated in weekly sports activities and, on 10 April 2023, took part in an event at which several inmates celebrated Ramadan together.

33. It was not in dispute between the parties that the third applicant had access to medical care. He was examined at the prison hospital several times and transferred to State hospitals when necessary. He underwent two assessments of his mental well-being upon admission to Silivri Prison, during which no issues were identified. He declined to meet the prison’s psycho‑social service psychologist on six occasions between 2016 and 2020 but did attend eight meetings with the psychologist after 2021. In the interview notes kept by the prison’s psycho-social service psychologist in respect of the six interviews which the third applicant had refused, it was stated that the applicant had been called to an interview for the purposes of psychological follow-up, but that he had not agreed to meet. As regards the interviews held with the third applicant after 2021, the psychologist noted that his post-release plans had been discussed, that in the course of those interviews his awareness of his offence had been addressed, and that he had declared that he had no links with a terrorist organisation. Interview notes drawn up in later meetings noted that they had discussed whether the third applicant’s links with the terrorist organisation had subsisted, and it was noted that the applicant had stated that he felt remorse about the situation in which he found himself. On 1 November 2018 he consulted a psychiatrist at the State hospital in Silivri Prison, who noted that he was experiencing difficulty arising from his being held in a single cell, diagnosed him with adjustment disorder and prescribed medication. The third applicant, for his part, submitted that he had been diagnosed with a stress disorder in 2018 and had been prescribed antidepressant medication.
Application no. 34616/21 (İlhan Akıllı v. Türkiye)

34. The applicant in application no. 34616/21 (hereinafter referred to as “the fourth applicant”) was a public prosecutor in Eskişehir at the time of his arrest. On 17 July 2016 he was arrested on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY. On 21 July 2017 he was placed in pre-trial detention in Eskişehir H-Type Prison where he remained until his release on 6 February 2018.

35. On 19 September 2016 the prison’s administration and observation board decided to remove the fourth applicant from the multi-occupancy cell in which he was being held and to place him in a single cell, stating that this was required for institutional security, in view of information obtained through internal intelligence gathered within the institution.

36. The fourth applicant lodged an objection with the enforcement judge against the prison administration’s decision, submitting that the isolation imposed on him was contrary to the law and that the decision had had an adverse effect on his psychological state. In its observations to the enforcement judge, the prison administration stated that the fourth applicant had been placed in a single cell on grounds of institutional security, that he was allowed 30 minutes of outdoor exercise per day, and that steps were being taken with a view to extending that period. On 6 December 2016 the enforcement judge dismissed the fourth applicant’s objection, finding the prison administration’s decision to be in conformity with the law and standard procedure. On 14 December 2016 the Eskişehir Assize Court rejected an objection lodged by the fourth applicant against that decision. On 23 January 2017 the fourth applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, arguing that his isolation from the rest of the prison population had been unlawful and had violated the prohibition on ill‑treatment.

37. On 13 October 2020 the Constitutional Court declared the fourth applicant’s individual application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded. In its decision, the court considered that the fourth applicant had been held in a single cell for one year and eight months; that the cells had been of an adequate size according to the European Prison Rules, that he had had unrestricted access to family visits, telephone calls and lawyer meetings, and that he had benefited from daily outdoor exercise of the duration of one hour, which he had undertaken alone for 15 months. It concluded that the conditions and duration complained of did not exceed the minimum severity threshold under the prohibition of ill‑treatment. This decision was notified to the applicant on 3 December 2020.

38. Following his placement in the single cell, between 27 September 2016 and 2 February 2017 the fourth applicant addressed several letters to the prison administration, requesting that his conditions of detention be improved. He requested, inter alia, the annulment of the decision placing him in a single cell and that he be returned to a multi-occupancy cell. Alternatively, he requested that he be allowed to take outdoor exercise in the company of another detainee, S.Y., who was subject to the same measure, or that the prison administration designate another detainee with whom he could take daily outdoor exercise. He further requested the extension of his daily outdoor exercise time to one hour and that his weekly telephone call be moved to a Saturday.

39. On 20 February 2017 the prison administration rejected the fourth applicant’s request to be returned to a multi-occupancy cell, deeming that the grounds for his placement in a single cell continued to apply and that his being held there did not pose any serious threat to his physical or mental integrity. It also rejected his request for joint outdoor exercise with S.Y. or another detainee on the grounds that allowing him to take exercise with another detainee facing prosecution on the same charge of membership of the FETÖ/PDY would facilitate intra-organisational communication and create a security risk. The administration accepted, however, his requests for his weekly telephone call to be rescheduled to a Saturday and for his daily outdoor exercise time to be extended to one hour.

40. On 26 July 2017 the fourth applicant once again requested that he be accommodated in a multiple-occupancy cell. On 11 August 2017 the prison administration rejected that request, stating that the grounds for the fourth applicant’s placement in a single cell remained valid. Objections lodged by the fourth applicant against that decision were rejected by the enforcement judge and the Eskişehir Assize Court.

41. From 19 September 2016 until his release on 6 February 2018, the fourth applicant was held in six different single-occupancy cells with total surface areas ranging between 7.98 sq. m and 12.17 sq. m.

42. The parties disagreed in respect of outdoor exercise. The Government submitted that throughout the period the fourth applicant had had access to the outdoor area for one hour a day. The fourth applicant submitted that between 19 September 2016 and 6 May 2017 – a period of some eight months – he had been taken to the outdoor yard for only 30 minutes a day, alone and in a completely separate section that had afforded no opportunity for human interaction. The fourth applicant submitted in this connection that his requests and applications to the prison administration had gone unanswered. Only after he had lodged a criminal complaint against the prison officials had the administration, on 20 February 2017, granted him one hour of daily outdoor exercise (see paragraph 39 above). That decision had been implemented only on 6 May 2017, and he had thereafter been able to access the yard with one or two other inmates for one hour a day. The fourth applicant submitted that he had not been allowed to participate in any social or sports activities during the period in question. The Government did not submit any information demonstrating that the fourth applicant had participated in any such activities.

43. The fourth applicant received visits from his relatives and lawyers on 66 different days, with several relatives sometimes attending on the same day, and had telephone calls with relatives on 34 occasions. The parties disagreed in respect of the fourth applicant’s access to reading material and activities: the Government submitted that he had had access to periodical and non‑periodical publications and had borrowed 68 books during his detention, whereas the fourth applicant submitted that throughout his detention he had been denied access to educational, sporting or religious services, that his access to books and television had been delayed, and that a radio he had bought from the prison canteen had been confiscated.

44. The fourth applicant was examined by the prison doctor on multiple occasions in connection with various physical complaints (for which medication was prescribed and provided) and was referred for a cardiological examination at Eskişehir State Hospital in May 2017, where no pathology was identified. As regards his psychological condition, he was referred to the prison psychiatrist on 27 October 2016 and was subsequently diagnosed with anxiety disorder and depressive episodes, his prescriptions being adjusted at follow-up examinations. The fourth applicant submitted that during this time he had suffered from anxiety and depression.
RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
Law no. 5275 of 13 December 2004 on the enforcement of sentences and preventive measures

45. Law no. 5275 sets out the rules with respect to the enforcement of sentences and detention in prisons. It regulates the placement of convicted prisoners in prisons; however, it contains no specific provisions regarding the placement of remand prisoners. Under sections 24, 49 and 69 of Law no. 5275, convicted prisoners are grouped and placed in prisons according to their age, sex, the length of the prison sentence imposed, the nature of the offence of which they have been convicted and other relevant criteria (see X v. Turkey, no. 24626/09, § 23, 9 October 2012, and İlerde and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 35614/19 and 10 others, § 107, 5 December 2023). Nevertheless, while the provisions set out in the Law refer to “convicted prisoners”, by virtue of section 116, most of those provisions are applicable, mutatis mutandis, to remand prisoners in prisons, unless otherwise stated. The relevant provisions read as follows:
High-security closed penal institutions

“(1) High-security closed penal institutions are facilities which have internal and external security personnel [and which] are equipped with technical, mechanical, electronic and physical barriers against escape, where the doors of rooms and corridors are kept locked at all times, where contact between convicted prisoners outside their own room and with the outside environment is permitted only in cases specified by legislation, and in which convicted prisoners subject to a strict security regime are accommodated in rooms for one or three persons. In these institutions, individual or group rehabilitation methods shall be applied.

(2) The sentences of those sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment, as well as – regardless of the length of sentence – those convicted of establishing or directing an organisation for the purpose of committing offences (or ... within the framework of the activities of such an organisation) [those] convicted of the following offences set out in the Criminal Code:
(d) offences against the security of the State (Articles 302, 303, 304, 307, 308),
(e) offences against the constitutional order and the functioning of this order (Articles 309, 310, 311, 312, 313, 314, 315),
shall be served in these institutions”
Classification of convicted prisoners
“Convicted prisoners shall be divided into groups such as:
(a) first-time offenders, recidivists, habitual offenders, or those who have made a profession of committing offences;
(b) those who, owing to their mental or physical condition or their age, must be subject to a special regime of execution;
(c) those considered dangerous;
(e) offenders who are members of criminal organisations or of criminal organisations established for profit.”
Execution of a sentence of aggravated life imprisonment
“The principles pertaining to the execution regime for aggravated life imprisonment are set out below:
(a) the convicted person shall be accommodated in a single cell;
(b) the convicted person shall have the right to go outside and exercise in the open air for one hour per day;

“(1) The punishment of solitary confinement consists, depending on the nature and gravity of the convicted prisoner’s acts, of holding [the prisoner] alone in a cell, day and night, for a period of one to twenty days and depriving him or her of all kinds of contact, without prejudice to the right to go outdoors.
(4) The cell shall be arranged in such a way as to meet vital needs.
(5) A convicted prisoner placed in a cell shall not be prevented from communicating with official and authorised authorities or with his or her lawyer.”
Institutions in which detention orders are executed

“Remand prisoners whose acts and conduct fall within the scope of Section 9 shall be accommodated in high-security remand prisons or, where this is not possible, in the sections reserved for remand prisoners in high-security closed penal institutions.”

“Depending on [room] availability, detainees shall be housed in separate rooms depending on the types of offences [of which they have been accused] and the security risk they present. Those who are on bad terms [with each other] and those who were accomplices in committing an offence shall not be housed in the same rooms, and measures shall be taken to prevent them from contacting each other.”

“The following measures may be applied by the public prosecutor during the investigation stage, and by the judge or the court during the trial stage, in respect of detainees who are in a dangerous state, who present a risk of tampering with evidence, who endanger the purpose of the investigation or the security of the prison, or whose conduct is such as to allow the offence to be repeated:

CASE-LAW of THE CONSTITUTIONAL court
50. The Government provided the Court with the following case‑law examples with respect to the Constitutional Court’s practice.
Case of Raşit Konya (B. No. 2017/26780, 28 June 2018)

51. The individual application in this case concerned a remand prisoner who had been detained on charges of membership of FETÖ/PDY. After being placed in multi-occupancy cells for a certain duration, the prison’s administration and observation board decided to place the applicant in a single cell. It stated that his placement in that cell was aimed at ensuring safety and order within the prison facility and the safety of Mr Konya himself (in the light of his former profession). He was held in that cell for 13 days, after which he was assigned back to his previous multiple-occupancy cell. Mr Konya’s objections against the prison administration’s decision were rejected by the enforcement judge and the Kırıkkale Assize Court.

52. In its decision, the Constitutional Court firstly set out the general principles applicable to the separation of a prisoner from other prisoners, taking into account the case-law of the Court on the subject. It emphasised the absolute nature of the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment and held that, as a manifestation of that prohibition, the conditions provided to convicted prisoners or remand prisoners in the execution of a conviction or detention order had to be such as to preserve respect for human dignity. Accordingly, the manner of the execution of sentences and the conduct displayed by prison authorities during the execution process should not subject prisoners to distress or hardship of an intensity exceeding the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in deprivation of liberty.

53. Applying these general principles to the case, the Constitutional Court held, first of all, that prisoners’ placement in solitary confinement, or their separation from other prisoners did not in itself constitute a situation contrary to the prohibition of ill-treatment. It acknowledged that such practices could be applied for the purposes of maintaining discipline, on security grounds, or out of concern to protect a person held separately from other prisoners. Furthermore, the measure of solitary confinement could be applied not only out of concern for security or discipline, but also for purposes such as preventing prisoners from colluding in ongoing investigations or from cooperating with persons outside to commit a new offence. In examining whether accommodation in a single cell infringed the prohibition of ill‑treatment, the Constitutional Court noted that the conditions had to be considered as a whole, together with an applicant’s allegations concerning the specific facts, and that, in this context, the severity, duration, purpose and consequences of the measures had to be assessed jointly.

54. Examining Mr Konya’s complaints from this perspective, the Constitutional Court noted that, having regard to the size and facilities of the cell in question, it was clear that he had been held in conditions consistent with the European Prison Rules. Moreover, he had been allowed to use the open‑air exercise yard every day for two hours in the company of other prisoners. Having regard to the European Prison Rules, the Constitutional Court found that it could not be said that the two-hour daily period in question had been unreasonable. Accordingly, it found that Mr Konya had not been cut off from communication with other prisoners. Consequently, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible as manifestly ill‑founded, since the minimum threshold of severity had not been reached in respect of the conditions of detention complained of by Mr Konya.
Case of Timur Demir (B. No. 2018/33190, 9 May 2019)

55. The individual application in this case concerned a remand prisoner who had been detained on charges of membership of FETÖ/PDY. After being placed in multi-occupancy cells for a certain duration, on 10 October 2016 the prison’s administration and observation board decided to place the applicant in a single cell. Mr Demir’s objections against the prison administration’s decision were rejected by the enforcement judge and the Ereğli (Konya) Assize Court. At the time of the Constitutional Court’s examination, Mr Demir had been held in single cells for a total of 855 days.

56. In its decision, the Constitutional Court firstly reiterated the general principles applicable to the separation of a prisoner from other prisoners, taking into account the case-law of the Court on the subject, as noted in its Raşit Konya decision (see paragraphs 51-54 above). On the facts of the case, the Constitutional Court held, first of all, that having regard to the size and facilities of the cell, it was clear that Mr Demir was being held in conditions consistent with the European Prison Rules. Moreover, he was allowed to use the outdoor exercise yard every day for one hour in the company of other prisoners. Having regard to the European Prison Rules, the Constitutional Court found that it could not be said that that one-hour daily exercise period was unreasonable. Accordingly, it found that Mr Demir had not been cut off from communication with other prisoners. Additionally, the applicant’s right to receive contact and non-contact visits had not been affected by the decision to place him in a single cell. He was also able to have a television in his cell and to read periodical and non-periodical publications. Consequently, it declared the application inadmissible as manifestly ill-founded, since the minimum threshold of severity had not been reached in respect of the conditions of detention complained of by Mr Demir.
INTERNATIONAL INSTRUMENTS

57. The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (“the Nelson Mandela Rules”), A/RES/70/175 – the global key standards for the treatment of prisoners adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 17 December 2015 – provide as follows, in so far as relevant (footnote omitted):

“1. Where sleeping accommodation is in individual cells or rooms, each prisoner shall occupy by night a cell or room by himself or herself. If for special reasons, such as temporary overcrowding, it becomes necessary for the central prison administration to make an exception to this rule, it is not desirable to have two prisoners in a cell or room.

2. Where dormitories are used, they shall be occupied by prisoners carefully selected as being suitable to associate with one another in those conditions. There shall be regular supervision by night, in keeping with the nature of the prison.”
“1. Every prisoner who is not employed in outdoor work shall have at least one hour of suitable exercise in the open air daily if the weather permits.”
“1. In no circumstances may restrictions or disciplinary sanctions amount to torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
The following practices, in particular, shall be prohibited:
(a) Indefinite solitary confinement;
(b) Prolonged solitary confinement;

“For the purpose of these rules, solitary confinement shall refer to the confinement of prisoners for 22 hours or more a day without meaningful human contact. Prolonged solitary confinement shall refer to solitary confinement for a time period in excess of 15 consecutive days.”

“1. Solitary confinement shall be used only in exceptional cases as a last resort, for as short a time as possible and subject to independent review, and only pursuant to the authorization by a competent authority. It shall not be imposed by virtue of a prisoner’s sentence.

2. The imposition of solitary confinement should be prohibited in the case of prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their conditions would be exacerbated by such measures. The prohibition of the use of solitary confinement and similar measures in cases involving women and children, as referred to in other United Nations standards and norms in crime prevention and criminal justice, continues to apply.”

58. An extract from the section entitled “Solitary confinement of prisoners” in the 21st General Report of the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment of the Council of Europe (CPT), published in 2011 (CPT/Inf(2011)28-part2), explained what is meant by the notion of “solitary confinement”:

“The CPT understands the term ‘solitary confinement’ as meaning whenever a prisoner is ordered to be held separately from other prisoners, for example, as a result of a court decision, as a disciplinary sanction imposed within the prison system, as a preventative administrative measure or for the protection of the prisoner concerned. A prisoner subject to such a measure will usually be held on his/her own; however, in some States he/she may be accommodated together with one or two other prisoners, and this section applies equally to such situations.”

59. The same report also addressed different types of solitary confinement. In respect of solitary confinement as a disciplinary sanction and administrative solitary confinement for preventive purposes, the report noted:
“(b) Solitary confinement as a disciplinary sanction

Withdrawal of a prisoner from contact with other prisoners may be imposed under the normal disciplinary procedures specified by the law, as the most severe disciplinary punishment. Recognising the inherent dangers of this sanction, countries specify a maximum period for which it may be imposed. This can vary from as little as a few days to as much as a month or more. Some countries allow prison directors to impose a given maximum period, with the possibility for a judicial body to impose a longer period. Most countries – but not all – prohibit sequential sentences of solitary confinement.

Given the potentially very damaging effects of solitary confinement, the CPT considers that the principle of proportionality requires that it be used as a disciplinary punishment only in exceptional cases and as a last resort, and for the shortest possible period of time. The trend in many member States of the Council of Europe is towards lowering the maximum possible period of solitary confinement as a punishment. The CPT considers that the maximum period should be no higher than 14 days for a given offence, and preferably lower. Further, there should be a prohibition of sequential disciplinary sentences resulting in an uninterrupted period of solitary confinement in excess of the maximum period. Any offences committed by a prisoner which it is felt call for more severe sanctions should be dealt with through the criminal justice system.
(c) Administrative solitary confinement for preventative purposes

The law in most European countries allows for an administrative decision to place into solitary confinement prisoners who have caused, or are judged likely to cause, serious harm to others or who present a very serious risk to the safety or security of the prison. This may be for as short as a few hours, in the case of an isolated incident, or for as long as a period of years in cases involving prisoners who are considered as particularly dangerous and to continue to pose an imminent threat. This is potentially the longest lasting type of solitary confinement and often the one with the fewest procedural safeguards. It is therefore crucial that there be rules to ensure that it is not used too readily (e.g. as an immediate response to every disciplinary infraction pending adjudication), too extensively or for too lengthy periods.”

60. The CPT’s report entitled “Living space per prisoner in prison establishments: CPT standards”, published in 2015 (CPT/Inf(2015)44) explained the minimum standards established by the CPT regarding the personal living space in prison establishments. It recommended that a single cell should measure 6 square metres plus the space required for a sanitary annex (usually 1 to 2 square metres).

61. The European Prison Rules (Recommendation Rec(2006)2 of the Committee of Ministers to member States, adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 11 January 2006 at the 952nd meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies), as applicable at the relevant time and in so far as relevant, read:
“17.2 Allocation shall also take into account the requirements of continuing criminal investigations, safety and security and the need to provide appropriate regimes for all prisoners.

18.1 The accommodation provided for prisoners, and in particular all sleeping accommodation, shall respect human dignity and, as far as possible, privacy, and meet the requirements of health and hygiene, due regard being paid to climatic conditions and especially to floor space, cubic content of air, lighting, heating and ventilation.
18.5 Prisoners shall normally be accommodated during the night in individual cells except where it is preferable for them to share sleeping accommodation.
18.6 Accommodation shall only be shared if it is suitable for this purpose and shall be occupied by prisoners suitable to associate with each other.
18.7 As far as possible, prisoners shall be given a choice before being required to share sleeping accommodation.
