25.2 This [prison] regime shall allow all prisoners to spend as many hours a day outside their cells as are necessary for an adequate level of human and social interaction.
27.1 Every prisoner shall be provided with the opportunity of at least one hour of exercise every day in the open air, if the weather permits.
27.7 Prisoners shall be allowed to associate with each other during exercise and in order to take part in recreational activities.

43.2 The medical practitioner or a qualified nurse reporting to such a medical practitioner shall pay particular attention to the health of prisoners held under conditions of solitary confinement, shall visit such prisoners daily, and shall provide them with prompt medical assistance and treatment at the request of such prisoners or the prison staff.

43.3 The medical practitioner shall report to the director whenever it is considered that a prisoner’s physical or mental health is being put seriously at risk by continued imprisonment or by any condition of imprisonment, including conditions of solitary confinement.
51.4 Each prisoner shall then be held in security conditions appropriate to these levels of risk.
51.5 The level of security necessary shall be reviewed at regular intervals throughout a person’s imprisonment.
53.1 Special high-security or safety measures shall only be applied in exceptional circumstances.
53.2 There shall be clear procedures to be followed when such measures are to be applied to any prisoner.
53.3 The nature of any such measures, their duration and the grounds on which they may be applied shall be determined by national law.
53.4 The application of the measures in each case shall be approved by the competent authority for a specified period of time.
53.5 Any decision to extend the approved period of time shall be subject to a new approval by the competent authority.
53.6 Such measures shall be applied to individuals and not to groups of prisoners.
53.7 Any prisoner subjected to such measures shall have a right of complaint in the terms set out in Rule 70.
60.5 Solitary confinement shall be imposed as a punishment only in exceptional cases and for a specified period of time, which shall be as short as possible.”

62. The European Prison Rules were revised and amended by the Committee of Ministers on 1 July 2020 at the 1380th meeting of the Ministers’ Deputies. The contemporary European standards on the separation of a prisoner from other prisoners as a special high-security or safety measure, as well as solitary confinement – set out in Rules 53A and 60 of the revised European Prison Rules – provide as follows:
“53A The following provisions apply to the separation of a prisoner from other prisoners as a special high security or safety measure:
a. prisoners who are separated shall be offered at least two hours of meaningful human contact a day;

b. the decision on separation shall take into account the state of health of the prisoners concerned and any disabilities they may have which may render them more vulnerable to the adverse effects of separation;
c. separation shall be used for the shortest period necessary to achieve its objectives and shall be regularly reviewed in line with these objectives;
d. prisoners who are separated shall not be subject to further restrictions beyond those necessary for meeting the stated purpose of such separation;
e. cells used for separation shall meet the minimum standards applicable in these rules to other accommodation for prisoners;

f. the longer a prisoner is separated from other prisoners, the more steps shall be taken to mitigate the negative effects of their separation by maximising their contact with others and by providing them with facilities and activities;
g. prisoners who are separated shall be provided, as a minimum, with reading materials and the opportunity to exercise for one hour per day, as specified for prisoners in Rules 27.1 and 27.2;
h. prisoners who are separated shall be visited daily, including by the director of the prison or by a member of staff acting on behalf of the director of the prison;
i. when separation is adversely affecting a prisoner’s physical or mental health, action shall be taken to suspend it or to replace it with a less restrictive measure;
j. any prisoner who is separated shall have a right of complaint in the terms set out in Rule 70.

60.6.a Solitary confinement, that is the confinement of a prisoner for more than 22 hours a day without meaningful human contact, shall never be imposed on children, pregnant women, breastfeeding mothers or parents with infants in prison.

60.6.b The decision on solitary confinement shall take into account the current state of health of the prisoner concerned. Solitary confinement shall not be imposed on prisoners with mental or physical disabilities when their condition would be exacerbated by it. Where solitary confinement has been imposed, its execution shall be terminated or suspended if the prisoner’s mental or physical condition has deteriorated.

60.6.c Solitary confinement shall not be imposed as a disciplinary punishment, other than in exceptional cases and then for a specified period, which shall be as short as possible and shall never amount to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.
60.6.d The maximum period for which solitary confinement may be imposed shall be set in national law.

60.6.e Where a punishment of solitary confinement is imposed for a new disciplinary offence on a prisoner who has already spent the maximum period in solitary confinement, such a punishment shall not be implemented without first allowing the prisoner to recover from the adverse effects of the previous period of solitary confinement.
60.6.f Prisoners who are in solitary confinement shall be visited daily, including by the director of the prison or by a member of staff acting on behalf of the director of the prison.”
JOINDER OF THE APPLICATIONS
63. Having regard to the similar subject matter of the applications, the Court finds it appropriate to examine them jointly in a single judgment.
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 3 OF THE CONVENTION

64. The applicants complained under Article 3 of the Convention that their placement in single cells and the restrictions imposed on their contact with other prisoners had violated their right not to be subjected to inhuman or degrading treatment. The fourth applicant also complained under Article 13 of the Convention that there were no effective remedies by which to challenge the prison administration’s decision to place him in a single cell. Being the master of the characterisation to be given in law to the facts of the case (see Radomilja and Others v. Croatia [GC], nos. 37685/10 and 22768/12, §§ 114, 124 and 126, 20 March 2018), the Court considers that that complaint falls to be examined only under Article 3 of the Convention, which reads:
“No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.”

65. The Government did not raise any pleas of inadmissibility in respect of the applications lodged by the first, third and fourth applicants. However, they invited the Court to declare certain parts of the complaints of the second applicant inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies.

66. In this regard, the Government submitted that his complaints concerning his placement in a single cell should be divided into two parts: the period during which he had been held in Samsun Prison (between 19 September 2016 and 15 November 2016 – see paragraphs 17 and 18 above) and the period in Bolu Prison (between 18 November 2017 and 8 October 2020 – see paragraph 22 above). They submitted that second applicant had not lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court after the Samsun enforcement judge had rejected his objection to the prison administration’s decision to place him in a single cell (see paragraph 17 above). They accordingly requested the Court to declare the second applicant’s complaint inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in so far as it concerned the period during which he had been held in Samsun Prison.
67. The second applicant did not comment on the Government’s arguments regarding the admissibility of this complaint.

68. The general principles with regard to the exhaustion of domestic remedies may be found in Vučković and Others v. Serbia ((preliminary objection) [GC], nos. 17153/11 and 29 others, §§ 69-77, 25 March 2014), Communauté genevoise d’action syndicale (CGAS) v. Switzerland ([GC], no. 21881/20, §§ 138-145, 27 November 2023), and Duarte Agostinho and Others v. Portugal and 32 Others ((dec.) [GC], no. 39371/20, § 215, 9 April 2024).

69. As regards the Government’s objection in the second applicant’s case, the Court firstly observes that after spending approximately two months in a single cell in Samsun Prison (between 19 September 2016 and 15 November 2016 – see paragraphs 17-18 above), the applicant was transferred to Bolu Prison on 15 November 2016, where he was placed in a multiple-occupancy cell. Approximately one year later, on 18 November 2017, he was placed in a single cell in Bolu Prison (see paragraph 18 above). The two periods of his detention in a single cell were therefore separated by an interval of approximately one year during which the second applicant was detained under materially different conditions.

70. The Court further observes that the second applicant did not lodge an individual application with the Constitutional Court following the rejection of his objection by the Samsun Assize Court on 17 October 2016 (see paragraph 17 above) but did so only on 4 September 2018 – that is, after the rejection of his objection by the Bolu Assize Court (see paragraph 20 above). The substance of his grievance concerning his placement in a single cell in Samsun Prison was therefore not brought before the Constitutional Court within the required 30-day time-limit. The fact that he subsequently referred to the period in Samsun Prison in the individual application that he lodged in respect of his later detention in Bolu Prison (see paragraph 21 above) cannot remedy that omission, since by then the time-limit applicable to the grievance regarding the conditions in Samsun Prison had long expired.

71. The Court reiterates that an applicant who has not complied with the procedural requirements governing a domestic remedy (including the applicable time-limits) cannot be regarded as having properly exhausted that remedy for the purposes of Article 35 § 1 of the Convention (see Vučković and Others, cited above, § 72). It also reiterates that when domestic courts have examined the substance of an applicant’s complaint, the applicant cannot be said to have failed to exhaust domestic remedies (see Verein gegen Tierfabriken Schweiz (VgT) v. Switzerland (no. 2) [GC], no. 32772/02, §§ 43‑45, ECHR 2009; Voggenreiter v. Germany (dec.), no. 47169/99, 28 November 2002; and Sungur v. Türkiye, no. 56462/19, § 52, 17 March 2026). In that regard, the Court notes that although the Constitutional Court did not reject the second applicant’s complaint concerning his conditions of detention in Samsun Prison for being out of time, it rejected his individual application using a standard formula encompassing all the grounds of inadmissibility, which was similar to the one used by the Court itself (compare Hastaoğlu v. Türkiye, no. 29061/21, § 59, 7 October 2025). Accordingly, the Court cannot conclude that the Constitutional Court examined the merits of that complaint. Therefore, the mere fact that the Constitutional Court did not explicitly declare the second applicant’s complaint regarding Samsun Prison inadmissible for failure to comply with the 30-day time-limit does not prevent the Court from examining the Government’s objection and, where appropriate, rejecting the application on that ground (ibid., §§ 60‑61).

72. The Court finds that in view of his failure to comply with the time‑limit before the Constitutional Court for his complaint concerning his placement in a single cell in Samsun Prison (see paragraph 69 above), the second applicant cannot be regarded as having properly exhausted the domestic remedies in respect of that complaint. The Government’s objection should therefore be upheld and the application of the second applicant, in so far as it concerns the conditions of his detention in a single cell in Samsun Prison between 19 September 2016 and 15 November 2016, must be declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, pursuant to Article 35 §§ 1 and 4 of the Convention.

73. The Court notes that the remainder of the applications are neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. They must therefore be declared admissible.

74. All the applicants submitted that their placement and prolonged detention in single cells had amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment, in breach of Article 3 of the Convention. They maintained that the regime to which they had been subjected had constituted solitary confinement within the meaning of the Court’s case-law and had gone beyond the threshold of severity inherent in lawful detention. They further submitted that the decisions to place them in single cells had been devoid of any specific or individualised justification, rested on an abstract invocation of security grounds, and had therefore been arbitrary.

75. The first and second applicants submitted that no disciplinary sanction had been imposed on them and that there had been no incident or disciplinary proceedings during their detention capable of justifying such a measure, their records noting no violent incidents. Similarly, the third applicant submitted that his placement had not in reality been motivated by security considerations. In this connection, he referred to a news article published in November 2016 reporting that the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor had stated that the alleged ringleaders of FETÖ/PDY had been separated from the rest of the group “in order to break the resistance of FETÖ members”; the third applicant submitted that this statement demonstrated that the measure had not been based on any conduct attributable to him but had been deliberately intended to inflict psychological suffering.

76. The third and fourth applicants submitted that the decision placing them in single cells had been served on them only after they had already been moved there and that their objections had been dismissed without any reasoned assessment. The second applicant submitted that his isolation had at no point been the subject of any meaningful, individualised or periodic review.

77. The first, third and fourth applicants further submitted that they had been held in cells of the type used for disciplinary punishment or for prisoners serving aggravated life imprisonment, which in their submission revealed the punitive character of the measure.
78. The second, third and fourth applicants submitted that the maintenance of their right to family visits and telephone calls had not attenuated the severity of the isolation regime imposed on them.

79. The first applicant submitted that the material conditions of his cell had fallen short of the minimum standards of hygiene and human dignity. He also argued that his pre-existing conditions, such as his herniated disc, allergies, and groin pain had worsened due to the conditions in his cell and that being held in isolation had led to a deterioration in his mental health, causing severe depression. However, the authorities had not assessed the impact of his continued isolation on his health condition. The first, second and third applicants submitted that they had been subjected to nighttime checks, regularly disturbing their sleep.

80. The fourth applicant added that the outdoor-exercise regime imposed on him had been more restrictive than that applied to prisoners serving aggravated life imprisonment. He further complained that the cells he had been detained in had been small and that they had had no separate kitchen area, obliging him to wash his dishes in the bathroom sink.

81. The Government submitted, at the outset, that none of the applicants in the present cases had been subjected to the disciplinary penalty of solitary confinement. They stated that this disciplinary sanction, provided for in section 44 of Law no. 5275 (see paragraph 45 above), was a detention regime under which the prisoner was kept in a cell by himself or herself, for the whole day, and deprived of all contact, for a period of between one and 20 days, according to the nature and gravity of the acts concerned. They submitted that, by contrast, the applicants in the present cases had been held in single cells not as a disciplinary measure, but pursuant to room assignment decisions of the prison administrations. Accordingly, during their stay in the single cells, they had not been subjected to the restrictions on contact applicable to the disciplinary penalty of solitary confinement and had enjoyed all the rights afforded to other prisoners. In particular, while prisoners in solitary confinement were deprived of all contact, prisoners held in single cells retained their right to contact and non-contact visits, and to telephone calls. Furthermore, while prisoners subject to disciplinary solitary confinement could not have a radio, television, wardrobe, table or chair in the cell in which they were being held, the applicants had been allowed to have such items in their respective cells.

82. The Government further submitted that the applicants had been able to maintain their contact with both the outside world and other prisoners; therefore, they had not been subjected to social isolation. They had maintained sufficient contact with their relatives, lawyers, and other prisoners. Moreover, the material conditions of the single cells in which the applicants had been held had been compatible with Article 3 of the Convention. The Government accordingly submitted that no issues arose as regards the conditions of detention of the applicants. Therefore, they invited the Court to find that there had been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention.

83. The general principles regarding conditions of detention involving isolation were set out in Schmidt and Šmigol v. Estonia (nos. 3501/20 and 2 others, §§ 120-127, 28 November 2023), the relevant part of which reads as follows:

“120. Article 3 of the Convention enshrines one of the most fundamental values of democratic societies. Even in the most difficult of circumstances, such as when engaged in the fight against terrorism or crime, the Convention prohibits in absolute terms torture or inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment (see, among many authorities, Ramirez Sanchez v. France [GC], no. 59450/00, § 115, ECHR 2006-IX). Indeed the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment is a value of civilisation closely bound up with respect for human dignity (Bouyid v. Belgium [GC], no. 23380/09, § 81, ECHR 2015).

121. Ill-treatment must attain a minimum level of severity if it is to fall within the scope of Article 3. The assessment of this minimum depends on all the circumstances of the case in question, such as the duration of the treatment, its physical or mental effects and, in some cases, the sex, age and state of health of the victim (see Muršić v. Croatia [GC], no. 7334/13, § 97, ECHR 2016).

122. The Court notes that measures that deprive a person of his liberty may often involve an inevitable element of suffering or humiliation arising from a form of legitimate treatment or punishment (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 119). However, to fall under Article 3, the suffering and humiliation involved must in any event go beyond that inevitable element of suffering and humiliation connected with detention. The State must ensure that a person is detained under conditions which are compatible with respect for human dignity, that the manner and method of the execution of the measure do not subject him or her to distress or hardship of an intensity exceeding the unavoidable level of suffering inherent in detention, and that, given the practical demands of imprisonment, his or her health and well-being are adequately secured (see Muršić, cited above, § 99, and the cases cited therein). Furthermore, when assessing conditions of detention, account has to be taken of the cumulative effects of those conditions, as well as the specific allegations made by the applicant (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 119).

123. A prohibition on contact with other prisoners for security, disciplinary or protective reasons does not in itself amount to inhuman treatment or punishment (ibid., § 123, and the cases cited therein). While extended removal from association with others is undesirable, whether such a measure falls within the ambit of Article 3 of the Convention depends on the particular conditions, the stringency of the measure, its duration, the objective pursued and its effects on the person concerned (see Rohde v. Denmark, no. 69332/01, § 93, 21 July 2005, and Rzakhanov v. Azerbaijan, no. 4242/07, § 64, 4 July 2013).

124. The Court reiterates that solitary confinement without appropriate mental and physical stimulation is likely, in the long term, to have damaging effects, resulting in a deterioration in mental faculties and social abilities (see Razvyazkin v. Russia, no. 13579/09, § 104, 3 July 2012). Complete sensory isolation, coupled with total social isolation, can destroy the personality and constitutes a form of inhuman treatment that cannot be justified by the requirements of security or any other reason (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 123, and A.T. v. Estonia (no. 2), no. 70465/14, § 72, 13 November 2018).

125. Solitary confinement, even in cases entailing only relative isolation, cannot be imposed on a prisoner indefinitely and should be based on genuine grounds, ordered only exceptionally and with the necessary procedural safeguards and after every precaution has been taken (see Rzakhanov, cited above, § 73).

126. A system of regular monitoring of the physical and mental condition of a prisoner held in solitary confinement should also be set up in order to ensure its compatibility with continued solitary confinement (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 139, and Fenech v. Malta, no. 19090/20, § 66, 1 March 2022).

127. It is essential that a prisoner should be able to have an independent judicial authority review the merits of and reasons for a prolonged measure of solitary confinement (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 139 and 145; Onoufriou v. Cyprus, no. 24407/04, § 71, 7 January 2010; and Gorbulya v. Russia, no. 31535/09, § 77, 6 March 2014).”

84. The Court reiterates that in order to avoid any risk of arbitrariness, substantive reasons must be given when a protracted period of solitary confinement is extended. The decision should thus make it possible to establish that the authorities have carried out a reassessment that takes into account any changes in the prisoner’s circumstances, situation or behaviour. The statement of reasons will need to be increasingly detailed and compelling the more time goes by. Furthermore, such measures, which are a form of “imprisonment within the prison”, should be resorted to only exceptionally and after every precaution has been taken, as specified in paragraph 53.1 of the Prison Rules adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 11 January 2006 (see paragraph 61 above). A system of regular monitoring of the prisoner’s physical and mental condition should also be set up in order to ensure its compatibility with continued solitary confinement (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 139). It would be desirable for alternative solutions to solitary confinement to be sought for persons considered dangerous and for whom detention in an ordinary prison under the ordinary regime is considered inappropriate (ibid., § 146).

85. The Court has also examined – within the Turkish context – several cases concerning allegations of violations of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the imposition of restrictive detention regimes. In Öcalan v. Turkey ([GC], no. 46221/99, ECHR 2005-IV), it examined the restrictions imposed on Mr Öcalan’s contact with the outside world and the effects of his being the sole inmate in the prison. The Court considered that the justifications advanced by the Government – namely that the applicant was the leader of an armed separatist movement who might seek to take advantage of communications with the outside world to re-establish contact, and that his life would be difficult to protect in an ordinary prison – were not unfounded. It accordingly found no violation of Article 3. In Öcalan v. Turkey (no. 2) (nos. 24069/03 and 3 others, 18 March 2014), the Court found a violation of Article 3 in respect of the period prior to 17 November 2009, having regard to the considerable length of time during which the applicant had been the sole inmate of İmralı Prison, the absence of means of communication available to him, the restrictions on his access to news, and the deterioration in his mental state. It found no violation of Article 3, however, in respect of the period after 17 November 2009, by which time other prisoners were transferred to İmralı Prison and the restrictions imposed on Mr Öcalan’s contact with the outside world had been eased.

86. The conditions of detention in an F-Type prison were examined by the Court in Karakaş v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 68909/01, 9 November 2004). In that case, the Court dismissed the applicant’s allegations of solitary confinement, noting that he was not in solitary confinement, shared his cell with two other detainees, and received visits from his relatives.

87. In the case of Güngör v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 14486/09, §§ 25‑37, 4 July 2017), the Court assessed the compatibility with Article 3 of the conditions of detention of an applicant who had been imposed a 12‑day solitary confinement sanction under section 44 of Law no. 5275 (see paragraph 45 above) for possession of blunt objects in his cell. Having regard to the fact that the sanction in question was relatively short, not repetitive, and intended to ensure security inside the prison, the Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill‑founded.

88. In Karsu and Others v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 34971/05 and two others, §§ 69-79, 27 March 2018), the Court examined the detention regime of individuals who had been sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment. It found that, although the applicants (who were serving aggravated life sentences in single cells) were subject to restricted social relations, their isolation was neither sensory nor complete but merely relative, being capable of evolving over time according to the facilities available in the prison and the applicants’ own conduct. Finding that the applicants were able to participate in social and sportive activities in the prison and in view of their continued contact with the outside world, it rejected part of their complaint under Article 3 of the Convention as manifestly ill‑founded.

89. Lastly, in Bora v. Turkey ((dec.), no. 30647/17, §§ 22‑27, 28 November 2017), the Court examined an applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention in circumstances similar to the facts of the present cases. The applicant, who was a former judge held in pre-trial detention on suspicion of membership of FETÖ/PDY, had been placed in a single cell and complained of being held in solitary confinement. Having regard in particular to the length of the applicant’s detention at the time of the Court’s decision (approximately one year and two months) and noting that he was able to spend at least one hour a day in the outdoor yard shared with two other detainees, the Court considered that his conditions of detention did not attain the minimum level of severity required to fall within the scope of Article 3, and rejected this part of the application as manifestly ill-founded.
Application of those principles
General considerations regarding the applicants’ detention in single cells

90. The Court notes at the outset that the applicants in the present cases were not placed in single cells as a result of the imposition of a disciplinary sanction of solitary confinement on them, which was of limited and non‑recurring duration (contrast Güngör, cited above, § 35), but on the basis of administrative decisions taken by the prison administrations concerned (see paragraphs 11, 17-18, 28 and 35 above).

91. The circumstances of the present cases also differ in certain respects from those the Court has previously examined in the Turkish context (see paragraphs 85-89 above). The present applicants were charged with membership of an illegal organisation in the aftermath of the attempted military coup of 15 July 2016, without any specific determination by the domestic authorities that they were “dangerous prisoners”. As such, their cases were not comparable to that of the applicant in the above-cited cases of Öcalan, and Öcalan (no. 2), who was the leader of an armed organisation – a factor to which the Court had regard in assessing the justification for the restrictions imposed on that applicant. Nor were the impugned restrictions imposed within the context of a sentence of aggravated life imprisonment (contrast the above-cited cases of Karakaş, and Karsu and Others, § 70). While the present cases arise within a context similar to that examined in Bora (cited above, §§ 22-27), the restrictions at issue in the present cases were of longer duration and varied in their level of stringency.

92. Given that the applicants’ placement in single cells did not result from the imposition of a disciplinary sanction of solitary confinement (see paragraph 90 above), they were not subjected to the restrictions accompanying the disciplinary penalty of solitary confinement, as provided for by section 44 of Law no. 5275 (see paragraph 45 above). According to the information provided by the Government, which was not contested by the applicants, their contact with the outside world was not affected by the decision to place them in a single cell and they retained their right to receive contact and non-contact visits and to telephone calls at regular intervals (see paragraph 81 above). They were also able to have items such as a radio, a television, and a wardrobe, table or chair in their cells.

93. That said, the Court emphasises that, in the examination of the compatibility with Article 3 of the imprisonment regime imposed on the applicants, it is the nature, duration, justification and stringency of the regime in question, as well as its effects on the person concerned, that is at the focus of the Court’s assessment (see Sekour v. France, no. 52496/19, § 120 (ii), 12 March 2026), rather than its legal classification under domestic law. Furthermore, while a prisoner’s continued ability to maintain contact with the outside world is undoubtedly an important factor in the assessment of the detention regime imposed on an applicant (see Öcalan (no. 2), cited above, §§ 146 and 148), the retention of such visiting and contact rights is only one aspect to be taken into account in assessing those restrictions, and is not in itself decisive (see, for example, Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, §§ 143 and 161, where the Court considered that the applicant’s ability to receive occasional visits from his relatives and to make telephone calls to them – as well as the possibility of attending social programmes and of having meetings with an inspector or contact person, a criminal probation officer, a chaplain and medical professionals – had not been sufficient to alleviate the negative effects of repeated and extended periods of solitary confinement; Skachkov v. Russia, no. 25432/05, § 54, 7 October 2010, where the Court did not consider that the occasional meetings the applicant had had with his lawyer or family outside the cell had significantly altered the conditions of his detention, given that he had been confined to his cell all day, apart from one hour of daily exercise; and Rzakhanov, cited above, § 70, where the Court held that two long and six short visits from his family per year, or the occasional meetings the applicant had had with his lawyer outside the cell, could not have significantly altered the negative effects of his confinement to his cell for 23 hours a day).

94. As noted above, in the present cases the applicants were placed in single cells by decisions of the relevant prison administration and observation boards (see paragraph 90 above). In that regard, the Court notes that by virtue of the 2006 regulation, prison administrations were empowered to assign the rooms in which prisoners are to be held, having regard to such factors as the nature of the offence in respect of which the prisoner is detained, the prisoner’s prior profession, and the facilities available in the prison (see paragraphs 48-49 above). The Court further observes that, as a form of nighttime accommodation in an ordinary prison regime, “single-celling” is endorsed by international standards: Rule 18.5 of the European Prison Rules provides that prisoners should normally be accommodated during the night in individual cells, and the Nelson Mandela Rules set out a similar principle in Rule 12 (see paragraphs 57 and 61 above, respectively). The applicants’ placement in single cells cannot, therefore, in itself raise an issue under Article 3 of the Convention.

95. It is not disputed between the parties that the cells in which the applicants were held were equipped with a separate sanitary partition containing a washbasin, toilet and shower, and that the applicants had daily access to cold and hot water. They were furnished with a bed, mattress, wardrobe, table and chair. The applicants were able to buy a television and a radio from the prison canteen. They had access to the prison library and received periodical and non-periodical publications (see paragraph 8 above). As regards medical care, the applicants had access to the prison doctor and, where necessary, were transferred to State hospitals (see paragraphs 8, 15, 26, 33 and 44 above). The Court also notes that all of the applicants made ample use of their rights to visits and telephone calls, and maintained regular contact with their relatives and lawyers (see paragraphs 14, 24, 25, 32 and 43 above).

96. To the extent that first, third and fourth applicants submitted that their cells had been of the same type as those used for prisoners subject to the disciplinary sanction of solitary confinement (see paragraph 77 above), the Court considers that, having regard to the conditions described above (see paragraph 95 above), that circumstance does not, in itself, adversely affect the Court’s assessment of the material conditions of those cells.

97. That said, the Court notes that the crux of the applicants’ complaints concerns their separation from other prisoners following their placement in single cells, the resulting social isolation and their alleged lack of meaningful human contact. The Court reiterates in this regard that while removal from association with other prisoners for security, disciplinary or protective reasons does not in itself amount to inhuman treatment or degrading punishment (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 123, and Messina (no. 2) v. Italy (dec.), no. 25498/94, ECHR 1999-V), in assessing whether such a measure falls within the ambit of Article 3 in a given case, regard must be had to the particular conditions, the stringency of the measure, its duration, the objective pursued and its effects on the person concerned (see the above‑cited cases of Rzakhanov, § 64, and Fenech, § 65, as well as the case‑law cited in paragraph 93 above).

98. The Court also notes that the applicants were charged with the offence of membership of an armed terrorist organisation (see paragraphs 10, 16, 27 and 34 above). In placing the applicants in single cells, the prison administrations cited safety, security and administrative grounds, having regard to the nature of the offence with which they were charged, and their former positions as holders of public office (see paragraphs 11, 18, 28 and 35 above). The Court has held in similar cases concerning organised crime that the existing, continuing danger that an applicant may re‑establish contact with criminal organisations was an element capable of justifying even harsh isolation measures in order to exclude such a possibility (see, for instance, Piechowicz v. Poland, no. 20071/07, § 169, 17 April 2012, and Messina (no. 2) (dec.), cited above). The applicants having been detained on terrorism-related charges within the security context prevailing in the aftermath of the attempted military coup in Türkiye (see, mutatis mutandis, Mehmet Hasan Altan v. Turkey, no. 13237/17, §§ 89‑94, 20 March 2018), the Court finds that that consideration is equally relevant in their cases. Given these circumstances, the Court is prepared to accept that the imposition of some level of restrictions on the applicants’ contact with other prisoners was, in principle, justified in order to ensure safety in prison and to prevent the reestablishment of intra-organisational contact (compare Piechowicz, cited above, § 169).

99. However, it remains for the Court to address the question of whether the continued and routine restrictions on the applicants’ contact with other prisoners was necessary in order to achieve the aims pursued in each individual case and whether those restrictions were compatible with Article 3 of the Convention (see, mutatis mutandis, Piechowicz, cited above, § 170). Accordingly, the Court will examine, in respect of each applicant, the stringency of the restrictions imposed and whether the objective pursued justified their being put in place and then prolonged. When conducting this assessment on the applicants’ conditions of detention, account will be taken of the cumulative effects of those conditions, as well as the specific allegations made by each applicant (see, mutatis mutandis, Dougoz v. Greece, no. 40907/98, § 46, ECHR 2001-II, and Öcalan v. Turkey (no. 2), cited above, § 103).
The first applicant (Mr Musa Gökçe)

100. The Court observes at the outset that the first applicant was placed in a single cell on 17 April 2018 and remained there until his release on 14 July 2020 – that is to say, for a period of approximately two years and three months (see paragraph 11 above).

101. As regards the conditions of detention in his cell, the Court observes that the first applicant’s cell had a surface area of 12 sq. m. (see paragraph 13 above), which was in compliance with the standards recommended by the CPT (see paragraph 60 above). According to the information provided by the Government, which was not contested by the first applicant, the cell had a separate bathroom with access to a toilet and to hot and cold water at all times during the day (see paragraphs 8 and 13 above).

102. The Court notes the first applicant’s complaints in this regard that the physical conditions in the cell had fallen short of minimum standards of hygiene and human dignity. He submitted, in particular, that the bathroom in his cell had had no ventilation (giving rise to odour, mould and damp), that the toilet and the shower had been in the same space, and that he had been subjected to searches when going to the outdoor yard and had been subjected to nighttime checks (see paragraphs 13 above). However, having regard to the overall conditions in the single cell in which the first applicant was held, the Court considers that the matters complained of by the applicant cannot be regarded as reaching the minimum level of severity under Article 3 of the Convention in and of themselves (compare Bora, cited above, § 24).

103. Turning to the first applicant’s complaints concerning his isolation, the Court observes at the outset that the restriction on the applicant’s contact with other prisoners as a result of his placement in a single cell was based on the nature of the offence with which he was charged and his previous profession (see paragraph 11 above). The Court notes, that while reduced, the first applicant’s contact with other prisoners was not completely restricted. It is not in dispute between the parties that although the applicant spent 21 hours in his cell on his own, he was taken to an outdoor area twice a day (for one and a half hours on each occasion) in the company of two other prisoners. He was also allowed access to the grass pitch for one hour each week after July 2018, that is, three months following his placement in a single cell (see paragraphs 11 and 13 above). Given that the first applicant spent 21 hours per day alone in his cell and was able to associate with other prisoners for the remaining three hours, his detention regime did not meet the definition of solitary confinement under Rule 44 of the Nelson Mandela Rules and Rule 60 of the revised European Prison Rules (see paragraphs 57 and 62 above).

104. The Court also notes the duration of the applicant’s stay in the single cell, which lasted for approximately two years and three months (see paragraph 100 above). That duration, while considerable, must be assessed in conjunction with the stringency of the regime and the justification advanced for it. In this connection, the Court notes that the decision to place the first applicant in a single cell had no effect on his right to receive visits or right to telephone calls. His contact with the outside world thus remained unchanged (see paragraph 92 above). During his stay in the single cell, the first applicant was visited by his relatives and lawyers on 44 different days (several relatives sometimes attending on the same day) and had 88 telephone calls with his wife (see paragraph 14 above). In addition to retaining his right to communicate with his relatives, the first applicant also had access to books, and, as noted in paragraph 103 above, had access to the grass pitch on a weekly basis from July 2018 onwards (see paragraphs 13‑14 above). In the present case, the Court finds that the combination of these contacts, facilities and activities afforded the first applicant adequate mental and physical stimulation during the time he was detained in a single cell.

105. The Court considers that the level of the first applicant’s contact with other prisoners, together with the preservation of his external relationships and access to facilities and activities, ensured that the first applicant retained sufficiently meaningful human contact during the period in question. Given these circumstances, the Court considers that the restrictions imposed on him were not of such stringency as to require a more detailed justification than that which the authorities provided.

106. The Court also takes note of the first applicant’s complaints concerning the state of his physical and mental health during his detention. In particular, he submitted that pre-existing conditions, such as his herniated disc, allergies, and groin pain had worsened owing to the conditions in his cell. He further submitted that being held in isolation had led to a deterioration in his mental health, causing severe depression. He also maintained that no consideration had been given to the impact of his continued isolation on his condition (see paragraph 79 above).

107. As regards the first applicant’s physical health, the Court observes that he was able to access medical care for his complaints – including specific treatment for his herniated disc at the neurology and physiotherapy clinics (see paragraph 15 above). With respect to his mental health, the Court notes that the first applicant underwent two assessments of his mental well-being during the prison admission process. Throughout his stay in the single cell, he received individual counselling and was able to consult a psychiatrist at a State hospital. In this connection, the Court observes that some of the medical conditions of which the applicant complained were of a pre-existing nature, and that it is not in a position to establish, on the basis of the material before it, that they were caused or aggravated by his placement in a single cell. Having regard to the medical attention provided to the first applicant in respect of both his physical and his mental health, the Court is satisfied that the authorities adequately secured his health and well-being.

108. Taking into account these factors, the Court considers that the conditions concerning the first applicant’s placement in a single cell and the resulting limitation on his contact with other prisoners did not go beyond the inevitable element of suffering and humiliation inherent in detention (compare the above-cited cases of Öcalan (no. 2), § 148, and Rohde, §§ 97‑98). It therefore finds that the treatment complained of did not attain the minimum level of severity required for it to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention.
109. It follows that there has been no violation of that Article.
The second applicant (Mr Eşref Köse)

110. Having regard to its findings on the admissibility of the complaints of the second applicant (see paragraphs 69-72 above), the Court will confine its examination of the compatibility with Article 3 of the Convention of the detention regime to which the applicant was subjected to the period when he was detained in a single cell in Bolu Prison between 18 November 2017 and 8 October 2020 (see paragraphs 18 and 25 above). The Court notes that the duration of the contested detention was approximately two years and 11 months.

111. The Court observes that between 18 November 2017 and 1 November 2019 the second applicant was accommodated on his own in two separate cells which were designed to accommodate three persons – each with a surface area of 50 sq. m. From 1 November 2019 until 8 October 2020, he was placed in a single cell measuring 11.4 sq. m. (see paragraph 22 above). The second applicant did not raise any complaints regarding the material conditions of those cells, which are not in dispute between the parties. The Court therefore considers that the physical conditions in which the second applicant was held do not raise any issue under Article 3 of the Convention. As regards the second applicant’s complaint concerning the regular nighttime checks conducted by the prison officials disturbing his sleep (see paragraphs 22 and 79 above), the Court considers that this matter, in itself, cannot be regarded as reaching the minimum level of severity under Article 3 of the Convention (see paragraph 102 above and compare Bora, cited above, § 24).

112. Turning to the stringency of the restrictions imposed on the second applicant’s contact with other prisoners, the Court observes that, during his detention in single cells in Bolu Prison, the applicant was taken to the outdoor yard for one and a half hours each day in the company of another prisoner (see paragraph 23 above). From May 2018 onwards, his opportunities for inter-prisoner contact were significantly expanded: he was able to take part in social, sporting and conversational activities – including time on the grass pitch, the open pitch, the closed sports pitch, table tennis sessions and conversation groups – at regular intervals. While the prison administration restricted the applicant from participating in these programmes with other prisoners in September 2018, this decision was set aside by the Bolu Assize Court’s decision of 16 November 2018, and the second applicant continued taking part in social activities with other prisoners following that decision (see paragraph 24 above). According to the information provided by the Government, he participated in such activities on 28 occasions in 2018, on 56 occasions in 2019, and on 10 occasions in 2020. From 7 June 2018 onwards, he was also able to participate in psycho-social and cultural activities – including meetings with the prison’s preacher (see paragraph 24 above).

113. The Court observes that in placing the second applicant in a single cell, the Bolu Prison administration cited security and administrative grounds, having regard to the nature of the offence with which the applicant was charged (see paragraph 18 above). The applicant’s objection to that decision was examined by the enforcement judge and, on further objection, by the Assize Court (see paragraphs 19-20 above). The domestic courts took into account the Court’s case-law on this subject and its decision in Bora (cited above), and deemed the measure to be proportionate and necessary in view of the offence with which the second applicant was charged, the uncertainty as to his position within the criminal organisation, the risk that accommodation with co-accused might facilitate the re-commission of an offence, and the security of the institution. The Assize Court further had regard to administrative considerations relating to the prison’s accommodation capacity.

114. The Court observes that the regime to which the second applicant was subjected did not deprive him of all contact with other prisoners. Throughout the period in question, he was able to associate with at least one other prisoner during his daily outdoor exercise for 90 minutes. The Court notes in this connection that during the first seven months of his accommodation in a single cell, the second applicant’s daily inter-prisoner association was longer than that afforded to the applicant in Bora (cited above, § 22, where the applicant had one-hour daily inter-prisoner contact for approximately one year and two months). From May 2018 onwards, the restrictions on the second applicant’s contact with others were relaxed, as he had regular opportunities for further association with other prisoners through structured social, sporting and conversational activities. While the second applicant’s opportunities for inter-prisoner contact during the period in question (90 minutes per day with another prisoner) fell below the standard of at least two hours of meaningful human contact per day recommended for separated prisoners by Rule 53A of the European Prison Rules (see paragraph 62 above) and can be defined as solitary confinement under Rule 44 of the Nelson Mandela Rules and Rule 60 of European Prison Rules (see paragraphs 57 and 62 above), the Court considers that, taken together with the expansion of activities from May 2018 onwards, the fact that he was allowed to maintain contact with persons living outside the prison (including regular communication with his relatives and his lawyer), and the absence of any restriction on his access to facilities such as books and television, the second applicant retained a sufficient degree of human contact and mental stimulation throughout his detention (compare the above-cited cases of Ramirez Sanchez, § 150, and Rohde, §§ 97-98). In the Court’s view, the reasons advanced by the domestic authorities for the second applicant’s placement in solitary confinement – which took into consideration the nature of the offence with which he was charged and the security context in which the decision to impose that measure was taken (see paragraphs 19-20 above) – were sufficient to support the restrictions that were actually imposed on him.

115. As regards the second applicant’s complaint that his imprisonment had caused him psychological problems, the Court observes that, during the period in question, the applicant had sufficient opportunities to consult a psychologist and he received medication which was prescribed to him (see paragraph 26 above). Accordingly, the Court is satisfied that the prison authorities adequately attended to the second applicant’s mental health needs.

116. Having regard to the foregoing, the Court considers that the second applicant’s cell placement and the resulting limitation on his contact with other prisoners did not exceed the inevitable element of suffering and humiliation inherent in detention. The treatment complained of did not, accordingly, attain the minimum level of severity required for it to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention.
117. There has, accordingly, been no violation of that provision.
The third applicant (Mr Süleyman Kul)

118. The Court notes at the outset the discrepancy between the Government’s assertion that the third applicant had been placed in a single cell on 10 October 2016, and the third applicant’s submission that he had been accommodated in the same single cell as of 8 October 2016, following his transfer to the Marmara no. 4 L-Type Prison (see paragraph 27 above). In the absence of any information as to where the third applicant had been held between 8 and 10 October 2016, the Court accepts that he stayed in a single cell at the Marmara no. 4 L-Type Prison from 8 October 2016 until his release on probation on 7 June 2023, that is, for a period of six years and eight months (see paragraphs 28 and 30 above).

119. The Government noted that the cell in question measured 12.45 sq. m. The third applicant disputed that figure, submitting that the cell had in fact measured 8 sq. m. (see paragraph 30 above). The Court observes that the third applicant’s submissions in this regard are not precise and not based on objective and concordant proof. Therefore, they are not sufficient for the Court to set aside the information provided by the Government (see, mutatis mutandis, Ananyev and Others v. Russia, nos. 42525/07 and 60800/08, § 122, 10 January 2012, and İlerde and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 35614/19 and 10 others, § 173, 5 December 2023). The Court finds that, in any event, the size of the third applicant’s cell complied with the relevant CPT standards (see paragraph 60 above).

120. The Court also notes the third applicant’s further submissions regarding the conditions in his cell. In particular, he submitted that he had been woken hourly throughout the night by the switching on of the lights and had been exposed to permanent artificial light during the nighttime (see paragraphs 31 and 79 above). The Government did not make any submissions in that respect. Having regard to the Government’s failure to submit any evidence capable of contradicting the third applicant’s allegations, in circumstances where they undoubtedly have greater access to potential sources of evidence concerning this matter (see, mutatis mutandis, Ananyev and Others, cited above, §§ 122-23), the Court accepts the applicant’s account in this regard. While these factors, taken alone, would not suffice to establish a violation of Article 3 (see paragraphs 102 and 111 above), the Court observes that they nevertheless affected his quality of sleep, resulting in both physical and mental fatigue (see, mutatis mutandis, Yasak v. Türkiye [GC], no. 17389/20, § 244, 5 May 2026).

121. As regards the stringency of the regime imposed on the third applicant, the Court observes that between 8 October 2016 and 9 May 2018 – a period of approximately 19 months – the applicant had no contact with other prisoners (see paragraphs 31 above). He was taken to the outdoor yard alone, for one hour each day, and his sole human interaction during that period was provided by visits from his relatives. From 9 May 2018 onwards, the restrictions were relatively eased: the third applicant was permitted to take his outdoor exercise for two hours each day in the company of two other prisoners. From 2019 onwards, he was also able to use the football pitch for 45 minutes once a week. Having regard to the duration of the third applicant’s opportunities for inter-prisoner contact, the Court observes that his detention regime falls to be defined as that of solitary confinement under Rule 44 of the Nelson Mandela Rules (for the whole period in question) and Rule 60 of European Prison Rules (for the period between 8 October 2016 and 9 May 2018) (see paragraphs 57 and 62 above). Nonetheless, in view of the regular contact with the outside world that he was able to maintain, the third applicant cannot be considered to have been in complete social isolation; rather, his isolation was partial and relative (compare the above-cited cases of Messina (no. 2), and Ramirez Sanchez, § 135).

122. The Court further notes the third applicant’s submissions regarding the deterioration of his mental health as a result of his isolation. It observes in this connection that the third applicant’s access to medical care was not restricted during his imprisonment, and that he had in fact declined several meetings with the prison’s psycho-social service psychologist. However, the Court observes from the meeting notes drawn up by the psychologist that the main issues discussed in these meetings appear not to have concerned the applicant’s capacity to cope with his isolation, but rather on his awareness of his offence, any continued links with the illegal organisation, and his future plans. The Court further observes that following a consultation with a psychiatrist in November 2018, the third applicant was found to be experiencing difficulties with staying in a single cell, and was diagnosed with adjustment disorder, in respect of which medication was prescribed (see paragraph 33 above). Notwithstanding that diagnosis and the psychiatrist’s observation that the third applicant experienced difficulty about being accommodated in a single cell, the prison administration does not seem to have put in place any measures to assess the applicant’s psychological capacity to deal with long‑term solitary confinement or to consider its effect on his mental health. As a result, his accommodation in a single cell continued without interruption even after the psychiatrist’s assessment (compare Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, § 147, 28 November 2023). The Court reiterates in this connection that prisoners kept in long-term solitary confinement need particular attention in order to minimise the damage that this measure can do to them (see, mutatis mutandis, Razvyazkin, cited above, § 106 in fine; see also Rule 43.2 of the European Prison Rules, referred to in paragraph 61 above).

123. As regards the objective pursued by the authorities in placing the third applicant in a single cell, the Court observes that the prison administration took into account the nature of the offence in respect of which he was detained, and cited the need to ensure safety and order within the prison, as well as the applicant’s own safety owing to his former profession (see paragraph 28 above). In this respect, while the Court has accepted in principle that a certain level of restrictions on a prisoner’s contact with other detainees may be justified on account of the nature of the charges in question (see paragraph 98 above), it reiterates that the level of stringency of the measures applied must be necessary to achieve the legitimate aim pursued, and substantive reasons must be given when a protracted period of solitary confinement is extended (see, mutatis mutandis, Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 119 and 139).

124. In that regard, the Court notes that the reasons advanced by the authorities – which were generic in character and did not address the third applicant’s individual conduct or situation – cannot be regarded as sufficiently demonstrating the necessity of the continuous application of the restrictions imposed on him for a total period of six years and eight months. During that period, which the Court finds to be considerably long, the prison authorities did not reassess whether the continued imposition of the contested restrictions remained necessary (compare the above-cited cases of Ramirez Sanchez, § 139, and Piechowicz, § 177).

125. The Court accepts that, from 9 May 2018 onwards, the third applicant’s regime was materially eased, in that he was able to take outdoor exercise for two hours each day together with two other prisoners (see paragraph 121 above). As the Court has found in the cases of the first and second applicants, taken in isolation, that level of inter-prisoner contact would not ordinarily attain the threshold of severity under Article 3 (see paragraphs 103-105 and 114 above). However, the assessment under Article 3 must be made by reference to the regime taken as a whole, having regard to the cumulative effect of all the conditions experienced by the third applicant over the period in question (see Dougoz, cited above, § 46).

126. Having regard to the cumulative effect of (i) the very considerable duration of his accommodation in a single cell and the restrictions on his contact with other prisoners, totalling six years and eight months, of which the first 19 months involved no inter-prisoner contact at all; (ii) the adverse effects of the regular night-time interruptions to the applicant’s sleep through hourly checks; (iii) the demonstrated impact of the single-cell regime on his mental health; and (iv) the absence of any reassessment of the regime in the light of its objectives or its impact on the applicant’s mental health, the Court considers that the third applicant was subjected to suffering exceeding that which is inherent in detention (compare Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, § 163). The treatment complained of therefore attained the minimum level of severity required to bring it within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention and amounted to degrading treatment within the meaning of that provision.
127. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention.
The fourth applicant (Mr İlhan Akıllı)

128. The Court observes that the fourth applicant was placed in a single cell on 19 September 2016 and remained in six different single cells until his release on 6 February 2018 – a period of approximately one year and five months (see paragraphs 35 and 41 above). These cells measured between 7.98 sq. m and 12.17 sq. m. and – according to the information provided by the Government – were adequately furnished (see paragraphs 8 and 41 above). The Court notes the fourth applicant’s complaints concerning the cells being too small and that they had contained no separate kitchen area (see paragraph 80 above). However, having regard to the size of the cells in which the applicant was held, which were compliant with CPT standards, as well as the facilities available to the applicant in his room, the Court considers that the overall material conditions of the fourth applicant’s detention do not raise any particular issues under Article 3 of the Convention (compare Bora, cited above, § 24).

129. The Court further observes that the parties provided differing accounts of the stringency of the restrictions imposed on the fourth applicant during his stay in the single cells. The Government submitted that throughout the period in question the fourth applicant had been able to use the outdoor yard for one hour per day, without specifying whether he had been alone or with other prisoners (see paragraph 42 above). They also referred to the Constitutional Court’s findings, which stated in its decision in this regard that the fourth applicant was taken to the outdoor yard for one hour each day, which he had undertaken alone for 15 months (see paragraph 37 above). The fourth applicant, for his part, submitted that for the first eight months, he had been taken to the yard for only 30 minutes a day, alone, and that it was only from 6 May 2017 onwards that he had been able to use the yard with one or two other inmates for one hour a day (see paragraph 42 above).

130. In this connection, the Court notes that, by a decision of 20 February 2017, the prison administration granted the fourth applicant’s request for his outdoor yard time to be extended to one hour each day (see paragraph 39 above). Furthermore, in the proceedings before the enforcement judge, the prison administration itself acknowledged that the fourth applicant had been allowed 30 minutes of outdoor exercise per day, and that steps were being taken with a view to extending that period (see paragraph 36 above). In the Court’s view, the prison administration’s own submissions to the enforcement judge, together with its decision of 20 February 2017, were inconsistent with the Government’s submission – and with the factual finding made by the Constitutional Court – that the fourth applicant had had one hour of outdoor yard time throughout his detention in a single cell. Having regard to the consistency of the fourth applicant’s account, the corroboration provided by the prison administration’s documents, and the absence of any evidence from the Government substantiating their submissions regarding one-hour outdoor exercise, the Court finds the applicant’s account established. Accordingly, it will conduct its examination on the basis that, between 19 September 2016 and 6 May 2017, the fourth applicant had 30 minutes of solitary outdoor exercise per day, and that from 6 May 2017 onwards he had one hour per day with one or two other prisoners. The Court further notes that the fourth applicant was not allowed to participate in any social or sports activities during the period in question (see paragraph 42 above). Save for the one hour of yard time from 6 May 2017 onwards, his interpersonal contact consisted of his weekly visits and telephone calls with his relatives. In these circumstances, the Court finds that the restrictions imposed on the fourth applicant during the one year and five months in question were particularly stringent, qualifying as solitary confinement under Rule 44 of the Nelson Mandela Rules and Rule 60 of European Prison Rules (see paragraphs 57 and 62 above).

131. Regarding the initial eight months, the Court observes that the fourth applicant’s outdoor exercise, which was limited to 30 minutes per day during that period, fell below the minimum standard of one hour of daily outdoor exercise provided for in Rule 23 of the Nelson Mandela Rules and Rule 27 of the European Prison Rules (see paragraphs 57 and 61 above). The Court reiterates that of the elements relevant for the assessment of the conditions of detention, special attention must be paid to the availability and duration of outdoor exercise and the conditions in which prisoners may take it. It has frequently observed that a short duration of outdoor exercise limited to one hour a day was a factor that further exacerbated the situation of the applicant, who was confined to his cell for the rest of the time without any kind of freedom of movement (see, mutatis mutandis, Babar Ahmad and Others v. the United Kingdom, nos. 24027/07 and 4 others, § 213, 10 April 2012, and the cases cited therein). The Court considers that this concern applies with even greater force where, as during the first eight months of the period in question, the outdoor exercise was reduced to 30 minutes per day, and the fourth applicant had no human contact during it.

132. As regards the reasons advanced for the fourth applicant’s regime of imprisonment, the Court observes that the prison administration relied on grounds of institutional security based on intelligence obtained within the prison concerning the applicant (see paragraph 35 above). The enforcement judge accepted the prison administration’s reasoning without any further elaboration (see paragraph 36 above). The prison administration rejected several requests from the fourth applicant, whereby he had asked to be returned to a multi-occupancy cell, on the grounds that the reasons for his initial placement in a single cell continued to apply. They also rejected the applicant’s request to be allowed to use the outdoor yard in the company of another detainee, since that could facilitate intra-organisational communication and create a security risk (see paragraph 39 above).

133. In this respect, while the Court has accepted in principle that a certain level of restrictions on a prisoner’s contact with other detainees may be justified on account of the nature of the charges in order to prevent the re-establishment of intra-organisational contact (see paragraphs 98 and 123 above), it reiterates that the level of stringency of the measures applied must be necessary in order to achieve the legitimate aim pursued, and substantive reasons must be given when a protracted period of solitary confinement is extended (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 119 and 139). In the present case, the Court observes that the reasons advanced by the domestic authorities for the continuous application of the detention regime in question were abstract in character and did not engage with the fourth applicant’s conduct within the prison. In the Court’s view, they cannot be considered as sufficiently demonstrating the continued necessity of the stringent detention regime imposed on the fourth applicant (compare Provenzano v. Italy, no. 55080/13, § 156, 25 October 2018, and Horych v. Poland, no. 13621/08, § 102, 17 April 2012).

134. Having regard to the cumulative effect of (i) the duration of the fourth applicant’s accommodation in a single cell, totalling approximately one year and five months; (ii) the absence of any contact with other prisoners during the first eight months of his single-cell accommodation and the limitation of his outdoor exercise to 30 minutes per day during that time; (iii) the absence throughout the period in question of any opportunity to participate in social, sports or educational activities; and (iv) the abstract and non-individualised character of the reasons advanced for the continued application of the detention regime in question (as well as the absence of a substantive review of the measure by the domestic courts), the Court considers that the distress and hardship endured by the fourth applicant exceeded the unavoidable level inherent in detention. The treatment complained of therefore attained the minimum level of severity required to bring it within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention and amounted to degrading treatment within the meaning of that provision.
135. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention.
APPLICATION OF ARTICLE 41 OF THE CONVENTION
136. Article 41 of the Convention provides:

“If the Court finds that there has been a violation of the Convention or the Protocols thereto, and if the internal law of the High Contracting Party concerned allows only partial reparation to be made, the Court shall, if necessary, afford just satisfaction to the injured party.”
137. In respect of non-pecuniary damage, the third applicant claimed 50,000 euros (EUR) and the fourth applicant claimed EUR 85,000.
138. The Government contested those amounts, submitting that they were excessive and unjustified.

139. The Court accepts that the applicants must have suffered distress on account of the violations found above. Taking into account the duration of the periods spent by the applicants in solitary confinement, and making its assessment on an equitable basis, the Court finds it appropriate to award the following amounts, plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non‑pecuniary damage:
- EUR 7,000 to the third applicant;
- EUR 3,000 to the fourth applicant.
140. The third applicant claimed EUR 5,500 and the fourth applicant claimed EUR 10,790 for the costs and expenses incurred before the Court.
141. The Government contested those claims.

142. According to the Court’s case-law, an applicant is entitled to the reimbursement of costs and expenses only in so far as it has been shown that these were actually and necessarily incurred and are reasonable as to quantum (see, among many authorities, L.B. v. Hungary [GC], no. 36345/16, § 149, 9 March 2023). In the present case, regard being had to the documents in its possession and the amount of legal work necessary, the Court considers it reasonable to award EUR 1,500 each to those two applicants who claimed reimbursement in respect of the work carried out by their representatives in the proceedings before the Court, including other costs, plus any tax that may be chargeable to these applicants.
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT,
Decides, unanimously, to join the applications;
Declares, unanimously, the applicants’ complaints under Article 3 of the Convention concerning their being placed in single cells admissible with regard to the following periods:
From 17 April 2018 to 14 July 2020 in respect of the first applicant (Mr Musa Gökçe);
From 18 November 2017 to 8 October 2020 in respect of the second applicant (Mr Eşref Köse);
From 8 October 2016 to 7 June 2023 in respect of the third applicant (Mr Süleyman Kul);
From 19 September 2016 to 6 February 2018 in respect of the fourth applicant (Mr İlhan Akıllı);
Declares, unanimously, the remainder of the second applicant’s complaints inadmissible;

Holds, unanimously, that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention as regards the imprisonment regime to which the third and fourth applicants were subjected during the periods indicated in point 2 above;

Holds, unanimously, that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention as regards the imprisonment regime to which the first applicant was subjected during the period indicated in point 2 above;

Holds, by six votes to one, that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention as regards the imprisonment regime to which the second applicant was subjected during the period indicated in point 2 above;

that the respondent State is to pay, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final, in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, the following amounts, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement:
EUR 7,000 (seven thousand euros) to the third applicant, and EUR 3,000 (three thousand euros) to the fourth applicant plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non-pecuniary damage;
EUR 1,500 (one thousand five hundred euros) each to the third and fourth applicant, plus any tax that may be chargeable to them, in respect of costs and expenses;

that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amounts at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period, plus three percentage points;
