PARTLY CONCURRING, PARTLY DISSENTING OPINION OF JUDGE ARNARDÓTTIR

1. In respect of the first, third and fourth applicants, I agree with the findings of the majority of the Chamber. As regards the second applicant, however, while I agree that his complaints about the conditions of detention in Samsun Prison are inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies, I am unable to join the majority in their conclusion that the conditions of his detention in Bolu F-Type High-Security Prison did not attain the minimum level of severity needed to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention and that there has, therefore, been no violation of Article 3. As will be explained in more detail below, I find that the majority’s analysis in the second applicant’s case is out of step with developments in the Court’s case-law since Ramirez Sanchez v. France ([GC], no. 59450/00, §§ 117-20, ECHR 2006-IX) and with those under other instruments of international law.

2. The second applicant was imprisoned on 21 July 2016, originally in Samsun Prison. He was placed in relative solitary confinement in a single cell in Bolu Prison for a period lasting around two years and 11 months between 18 November 2017 and 8 October 2020. Apart from occasional family visits and limited organised social, psycho-social and cultural activities, his “meaningful human contact” during that time consisted of one and a half hours of outdoor activity with one other inmate per day. It should also be noted that the applicant did not take part in any organised activities until May or June 2018. This appears to have been the result of a ministerial circular of 28 July 2016, which stated that prisoners detained for membership of FETÖ/PDY should not take part in educational and rehabilitative activities until further notice. After the commencement of such activities, they were suspended again in the second applicant’s case between September and November 2018. The second applicant seems, therefore, to have been deprived of the possibility of participating in any organised social activities for eight to nine months during his detention in Bolu Prison. In respect of the social activities enjoyed for the remainder of the relevant period of detention, I also note that since the construction of the first F-Type prisons in the early 2000s, the European Committee for the Prevention of Torture and Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (CPT) has repeatedly drawn the attention of the Turkish authorities to the problem of the very limited communal activity programmes on offer (report by the CPT on its visit to Türkiye from 13-22 February 2024, 6 October 2026, CPT/Inf (2026) 35).

3. The question whether relative solitary confinement of the kind imposed on the second applicant reaches the minimum level of severity needed to fall within the scope of Article 3 of the Convention depends on the particular conditions of detention, the stringency of the contested measure, its duration, the objective pursued and its effects on the person concerned (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 117-20, and Schmidt and Šmigol v. Estonia, nos. 3501/20 and 2 others, §§ 122-23, 28 November 2023). In its assessment on the merits of Article 3, the Court’s task is to perform an overall assessment of the above factors and determine whether the implementation of the relevant prison regime was necessary as an exceptional measure, whether it was based on genuine grounds, whether sufficient safeguards against arbitrariness were in place and whether the authorities took appropriate precautionary measures to counterbalance the negative effects of solitary confinement (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 136, 139 and 145; Sekour v. France, no. 52496/19, § 120, 12 March 2026; Rzakhanov v. Azerbaijan, no. 4242/07, § 73, 4 July 2013; and Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, §§ 125‑27). I note in this respect that while the objective pursued by the contested measure may have an effect on the Court’s overall assessment of its necessity, the applicable principles are the same irrespective of whether the prisoner in question is held in solitary confinement for reasons of discipline or security.

4. In the application of the above criteria to the second applicant’s case, I find that the majority of the Chamber have not attached sufficient weight to the duration and intensity of his solitary confinement, which should, in my opinion, have placed the respondent Government under a heightened requirement to provide convincing reasons for the necessity of the imposition, and extension, of the measure.

5. In this regard I note, firstly, that the European Prison Rules were revised in July 2020 to include in Rule 53A(a) an express and unconditional requirement of at least two hours of “meaningful human contact” a day for prisoners subject to separation from others for reasons of security (Recommendation Rec(2006)2-rev of the Committee of Ministers to member States on the European Prison Rules). Rule 53A(f) further stipulates that the longer a prisoner is separated from other prisoners, the more steps shall be taken to mitigate the negative effects of their isolation by maximising contact with others and providing them with facilities and activities. Rule 44 of the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners (“the Nelson Mandela Rules”) of 2015, similarly, defines solitary confinement as 22 hours or more per day without “meaningful human contact” (UN General Assembly Resolution 70/175, 17 December 2015, 70th session, UN Doc. A/RES/70/175). Although the concept of “meaningful human contact” is not defined in these standard-setting documents, it is commonly understood as the amount and quality of social interaction and psychological stimulation which human beings require for their mental health and well‑being, which must take place in conditions that enable empathetic interpersonal communication (European Committee on Crime Problems (CDPC), Commentary on Recommendation Rec(2006)2-rev of the Committee of Ministers to member States on the European Prison Rules, CM(2020)17-add2, 1 July 2020). I take issue with the fact that the majority of the Chamber have considered the lack of two hours per day of “meaningful human contact” in the second applicant’s case to be compensated for by occasional additional human contact and access to facilities such as books and television. While this may be relevant for the assessment of whether he was subjected to complete sensory isolation or relative solitary confinement, it does not change the fact that he was deprived of the minimum two hours of “meaningful human contact” per day. I also find that the majority have disregarded in this respect the fact that the second applicant was deprived of the possibility of participating in any organised social activities for between eight and nine months during his detention in Bolu Prison. In addition, I note that the regular daily human contact he did enjoy was limited to interactions with one other person during outdoor exercise. This, in my opinion, required additional efforts on the part of the authorities to maximise meaningful contact with others, unless particularly convincing reasons justified the regime in question (compare N.T. v. Russia, no. 14727/11, §§ 44-46, 2 June 2020, where the Court considered placement with one other individual in a double cell comparable to solitary confinement).

6. Secondly, the second applicant’s solitary confinement, spanning two years and 11 months, was of significant length (compare Piechowicz v. Poland, no. 20071/07, §§ 170-73, 17 April 2012). In this respect, the present case is incomparable with the precedent relied on by the majority of the Chamber, which concerned solitary confinement for one year and two months immediately after the failed coup d’état of 15 July 2016 (see Bora v. Turkey (dec.), no. 30647/17, § 24, 28 November 2017). I also note that in Bora, the Court emphasised that its finding should not be interpreted as relieving the authorities of the requirement to ease the restrictions imposed as the length of detention increased (ibid., § 26). I further note that the second applicant’s prison regime included sleep disturbances and was harmful to his mental health. While access to mental health services and the provision of medication go some way towards ameliorating the negative effects of prolonged social isolation, this cannot in and of itself justify the continued placement in such conditions (see Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, § 147).

7. Turning, next, to safeguards against arbitrariness, I note that it emerges from international standard-setting instruments and the Court’s case-law that solitary confinement should be imposed only exceptionally as a measure of last resort and for the shortest possible period of time (see Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, § 134). Article 3 of the Convention, accordingly, requires that placement in prolonged solitary confinement should be based on sufficiently substantiated and genuine grounds, and subject to independent judicial review (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, §§ 136 and 145; Schmidt and Šmigol, cited above, §§ 125 and 127; and Sekour, cited above, § 120). In this respect, I note that the second applicant had shared a three-person cell with two other prisoners in Bolu Prison for a full year before being placed in a single cell on 18 November 2017. Taken together with the otherwise limited possibilities of “meaningful human contact”, this decision led to solitary confinement, which cannot be based on administrative convenience or stereotypical reasoning. On the facts of the second applicant’s case, however, there is nothing to indicate that the prison authorities’ decision to place him in solitary confinement for security reasons was based on an individualised assessment of his behaviour during the time he enjoyed more human contact, or new information about the security risk he might pose. The enforcement judge, who on 14 March 2018 dismissed the second applicant’s complaint about placement in a single cell, relied on the same stereotypical grounds related to the nature of the offence and security risks, while referring additionally to the “uncertainty as to his position within the FETÖ/PDY organisation’s hierarchy”. It is striking, however, that the second applicant, who had previously been a public prosecutor, had already on 18 January 2018 been convicted of the offence of which he had been accused. His role would therefore have been clarified by that time. Accordingly, the reasoning of the enforcement judge also indicates the absence of a genuine, individualised engagement with the second applicant’s actual circumstances and the potential security threat he posed. This was, furthermore, not remedied on appeal. The judicial review of the merits and reasons for the second applicant’s prolonged solitary confinement, therefore, proved to be ineffective.

8. Article 3 of the Convention also requires that decisions to extend solitary confinement must demonstrate that the authorities have carried out a reassessment of the circumstances and the prisoner’s conduct. The reasoning in support of solitary confinement must further become increasingly detailed and compelling as time goes by (see Ramirez Sanchez, cited above, § 139; Piechowicz, cited above, § 165; and Sekour, cited above, § 120). In the second applicant’s case, however, there is no indication that the decision to place him in solitary confinement had temporal limits or was subject to periodic review in the light of his behaviour or the evolving circumstances. In this regard, I note that the applicable domestic legislation does not seem to have secured any such regular review to prisoners placed in solitary confinement. This, in my opinion, is problematic in and of itself (see Sekour, cited above, §§ 129-33). In addition, even accepting that the authorities were justified in imposing a strict security regime on those detained on remand for suspected involvement in the failed coup d’état of 15 July 2016, or links with FETÖ/PDY, it must be noted that the level of their involvement with the organisation differed and was clarified in the ensuing criminal proceedings. The urgency of the security situation further diminished with the passage of time. Indeed, as amply demonstrated in the Court’s case-law, the authorities took swift, decisive and wide-reaching steps to curb the activities and influence of the organisation in Turkish society (see, for example, Bora, cited above; Yüksel Yalçinkaya v. Türkiye [GC], no. 15669/20, 26 September 2023; Onat and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 61590/19 and 6 others, 25 March 2025; İ.Ç. v. Türkiye, no. 48061/19, 13 January 2026; Kandemir v. Türkiye, no. 30906/19, 3 February 2026; and Yasak v. Türkiye [GC], no. 17389/20, 5 May 2026). It is also telling in this respect that the state of emergency declared by the Turkish authorities on 20 July 2016 was lifted on 18 July 2018. While the blanket ban on any educational and rehabilitative activities ordered by a ministerial circular for those detained on grounds of membership in FETÖ/PDY was first relaxed in the second applicant’s case around that time, he nevertheless remained in solitary confinement until 8 October 2020. The authorities’ knowledge of the second applicant’s psychological problems also provided additional impetus to review whether his solitary confinement was compatible with the requirements of Article 3 of the Convention. All the above elements demonstrate the evolving nature of the security situation and the second applicant’s personal circumstances, which called for careful reassessment (compare with automatic extensions based on stereotypical reasoning in Piechowicz, cited above, § 177, and contrast with the reassessments conducted in Sekour, cited above, §§ 123-24). In addition, as already mentioned, it is clear that the applicant was not considered such a threat to security that he could not be allowed more human contact in the year leading up to his solitary confinement and there is no indication that the authorities ever assessed whether his behaviour in prison posed a security risk. Taking all the above into account, I cannot but conclude that by depriving the second applicant of a regular and careful reassessment of the reasons for his prolonged solitary confinement, the authorities disregarded his well-being and the requirements of Article 3 of the Convention, effectively rendering the nature of the solitary confinement punitive rather than preventive.

9. In conclusion, therefore, I find that the minimum level of severity needed to engage Article 3 of the Convention was attained and that there has been a violation of Article 3 in the second applicant’s case.
